items.body:
Softly softly does it for the gorgeous debut duo of soundtrack composer Elori Saxl & saxophonist Henry Solomon with their lushly ephemeral grasp of 4th world ambient jazz, tipped for the anyone on the line between Lynch/Badalamenti, TLF Trio, Laurel Halo, Arve Henriksen or Alex Zhang-Hungtai's Love Theme side-wind.

Captured over a few days in LA, ‘Seeing Is Believing’ frames the sax player’s searching feel for tone across soundscapes sparingly coloured in subtle harmonic gradients by Elori Saxl’s fluttering Juno 106 keys. The nine parts are testament to the duo’s near-telepathic level of intuition and mutual vision of a palpably tissue-soft atmospheric music; one where spectres of ’70s minimalism and ’80s new age bleed forward into structures equally informed by soundsystem culture and contemporary pop production, achieving a sort of slow shifting, ecological pressure system that is a pleasure to sink into.

Within her richly visual, implicitly storytelling style, Elori Saxl draws on a wellspring of experience in composing for new music ensembles, and soundtracking and directing films for New Yorker and Slate, to set spacious dimensions for Solomon’s ruminative baritone sax and bass clarinet to wander freely. A quiet sense of restraint defines proceedings as their forms gently grow and sway from the dusky licks of ‘Reverence’ thru the gauzy lustre of the title piece, conjuring a geosmin waft in ‘Raindrops’ and LA hills panorama on ‘Reno Silver’, or balmiest breeze of Glass-like phrasing on ‘A Thousand Steps’, into the gorgeous, pitch bent and sensual sorcery summoned in standout ‘Heart.’

Stunner.

items.body:
Remastered for its 1st vinyl cut, The Bug aka Kevin Richard Martin’s immensely forlorn ’22 solo jag immures the senses in a slow-burn blizzard of white-out atonalities and infrasonic rumbles shot thru with an unnerving isolationist melancholia. One hard RIYL Thomas Köner, Mika Vainio’s elemental Ø works, or GAS, gone noxious.

Positively the bleakest thing he’s ever made, ’Sub Zero’ is a supremely powerful listening experience. Thry a dozen tracks Martin pushes the hallmarks of his work, under various guises and collaborations, to a logical conclusion of aesthetic and emotive obliteration. Effectively the heaviest ends of his work as part of EAR (with Porter Ricks’ Mellwig/Köner, Kevin Shields, Pete Kember), the dankest frequencies of The Bug, the detachment of ’Sirens’ (Room 40) and utterly heartbroken qualities of King Midas Sound, are collapsed into the sound of a luscious black hole succour, with a grasp of life-affirming heaviness that dangles it just above the end of the rope. 

Perhaps KRM’s finest, purest hour of aural haunting, the dozen tracks unfurl in glacial streaks on the imagination with a sense of scale and presence that pins heads in place, vulnerable to the elements. He continues to limn the void like he’s lived inside it and survived to tell the tale. A longhand conviction in dub-as-method guides him to the limits of that sound, where it crosses the threshold into realms shared by dark ambient, at the peripheries of BM, post-techno electronics and doom metal. In this atmospheric no-man’s-land he leaves an indelibly ambiguous impression, palpably stricken by existential dread but with pangs of beauty, as in the upswell of Eno-esque choral pads on ‘Too Human’ and ‘Higher Than the Sky’ that cling to hope like a limpet on the hull of his icebreaking structures. 

Magisterial stuff by an artist arguably in his imperial phase.

items.body:
Two hours and 20 minutes of music split across three LPs, Sarah Davachi's latest studio album is a milestone for what's best described as deep minimalism, placing string, brass and woodwind ensemble works alongside chilling Renaissance-style choral pieces and heady solo organ compositions. Absolutely crucial material for engaged listeners - you know the deal.

Now Davachi's always been better than just good. Even back in 2016 when she released 'Vergers' and 'Dominions', there was something about her vision of minimalism that set her apart from a dense crowd of drone phonies. It's what made 2025's 'The Head as Form'd in the Crier's Choir' so effortlessly engaging; by this point known as one of the most skilled composers in her field, Davachi imagined an album of psychedelic chamber-prog that crowned her already impressive discography, using the Orpheus myth as a metaphor for her own experiences - not looking back but moving relentlessly forward. So it's even more remarkable that she's able to follow up with an album as different and as monumental as 'The Will of Tongues'. On the surface, it's business as usual for Davachi, an album of restrained, early music-informed long-form compositions that builds on the foundations laid out by some of her more demanding material, like 2023's epic 'Long Gradus'. But there's more going here on than you might expect; ignore the eye-watering duration if you can, 'The Will of Tongues' is a record that rewards patience and attentive listening. It's an album that's about the act of listening itself, in fact, putting the listener in control of their experience. If you tune out, relegating it to background music, it'll sail over you like cherry blossoms in the wind, but lock in and its beating rhythms, stirring harmonies and precise tonal variations will unlock a door of perception you may not have even realised was there.

Take the opening track, 'Interlude I: Polyphonic, for Strings', performed by The Sung Blood Players - Whitney Johnson and Eyvind Kang on viola and Lucy Railton on cello - it's a study that's meant to limber up our senses for what we're about to hear. If you're not paying close attention, it's nothing more than an eight-minute drone, but concentrate and you'll hear the three voices diverge and converge in the most unexpectedly beautiful ways, creating vibrating resonances and oddball rhythms in the process. And similarly, on 'Canto Duo' Davachi introduces us to one of five pipe organs that have been "tuned in historical temperaments". This isn't an aesthetic flex, expected to trigger buried memories of church services and historical movies, it's a chance for listeners to marvel at the instrument's range and its ability to create wind tones that can't be easily replicated on any other instrument. Davachi plays slowly and methodically, letting her long pauses between notes form a structure that's replicated in a more micro scale by the psychoacoustic components that might only reveal themselves on the third or fourth run-through. And when the piece ends and Davachi waves in the Chamber Choir Ireland for the first of three 'Songs of the Smile's Fig' parts, what should be a radical shift in mood sounds instead like synchronisation: those slow rhythmic changes, now sung by six voices in a Renaissance-era polyphonic style, suddenly make perfect sense.

And the first big payoff comes right after Davachi introduces Phaedrus, the Switzerland-based Renaissance flute consort who perform 'Interlude V: Harmonic, for Woodwinds'. On 'The Second Tuning', our appreciation of the finer elements is rewarded with one of Davachi's most moving, harmonically rich compositions to date, a faded organ work that imagines history as a circle rather than a straight line, reflecting its stacked-up eras in slowly building, densely textured harmonies that keep on revealing their stirring complexity until the last notes. And we need this if we're going to muster up the stamina to absorb 'The Rose Dialogues', a 45-minute string composition that's split into two equal parts, hinting oh-so-subtly at romantic music but always zeroing in on those mysterious resonances, the sounds that Davachi's taught herself how to reveal by so carefully using space, tone and texture. What's remarkable for a record that's so lengthy and so coherent thematically, is that Davachi keeps showing her range. Even the organ pieces are recorded and arranged to display just how different the instrument can sound: 'Four Narrow Forms', for example, is ghostly and whimsical compared with the dense, breathy hum of 'The First Tuning'. 

Even the third of Davachi's 'Songs of the Smile's Fig' chapters is remarkable different from its predecessors, surreal and only faintly historical compared with the first part, each word seemingly lapping over the next to create an effect that's shockingly hypnotic. We can't even tell you another record that's quite like this, there are traces of Arvo Pärt, Éliane Radigue, James Tenney and Alvin Lucier of course, but at this stage, Davachi has cooked those raw materials into her own unmistakable sound, a form of deep minimalism that's not exactly mystical - it's psychoactive.

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)', on a new pressing for 2026.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like HTRK were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down into the abyss, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the drums become clammier while Jonnine's vocals drift like ghostly vapour trail. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, it's as good as it gets.

items.body:
The sixth album from New England alt-rock survivors Dinosaur Jr. since they re-emerged in 2005, 'There Near' is another rush of distorted, "classic" East Coast shreds that prove Lou Barlow and J Mascis still have what it takes.

There aren't many rock bands that can claim to match the sheer longevity and enduring quality of Dinosaur Jr. And somehow, record after record, they keep flying the flag for Massachusetts' mostly defunct alt-rock scene long after Sonic Youth (for years the presumed survivors) have dissolved, never to return. And the band's lyrics are still toothsome; Barlow takes aim at contemporary culture on the tongue-in-cheek 'Blowin' Up'. "There's nothing quite as bad as a boy edgelord," he quips. "The dreamin' and the schemin' that's so dark. Maybe you need a vacation?" On 'No Friends', meanwhile, Mascis confronts aging by writing one of the best grunge anthems Nirvana never wrote and blessing Murph's razor-sharp drums with screaming riffs courtesy of his newly-sourced 1970s Mesa Boogie MK1 amp - the same amp Chris Dixon has when Dinosaur Jr. recorded their first LP. "You always hear how Rick Rubin always makes bands he's producing sit down and listen to their first album and say let's get back to that sound," Mascis explains. "So I just gave myself this advice."

It's certainly a chunkier record than its predecessor, 2021's 'Sweep it into Space', an album that brought in Kurt Vile for production and extra guitar work. 'There Near' is tighter and still somewhat punkier - but like all of the records the trio have recorded since 2005, they don't try and re-invent the wheel. Mascis and Barlow are great songwriters and never really lose sight of that, simply finding better ways to present their thoughts and prolong their seemingly limitless momentum...

items.body:
A holy spirit of lowercase musics imparts waking dream sensations ​on his gorgeous debut bow for mutual souls, Students of Decay - keenly advised to new ears and his legion admirers alike, and lovers of The Caretaker, Timo Van Lujik, Tom James Scott, Eno, Akira Rabelais...

‘Mystical Obscurant’ is Chalk’s umpteenth LP in a catalogue famously spanning decades - from mid ‘80s post-industrial scapes as Feral Confine to this type of pinch-yourself dream material, under his own name and part of Elodie or Mirror - and yet it’s just as vital to longtime disciples as it is to new ears seeking a way into his sprawling body of work. Aptly offered by SoD as “a rare opportunity to encounter the expansive character of that oeuvre in miniature”, his suite of powdered timbral glisten and harmonic perfume ideally portrays a sound-sensitive knack for evoking atmospheric nostalgia with the barest ingredients, all spun out at deeply rested heart rate that stealthily comes to calibrate with your own.  

Each of the seven pieces feel as though they appeared from air, rather than performed by any physical being. The softness of his brush-stroke guitar and liminality of electro-acoustic sorcery shortens the gap between imagination and materiality with signature concision, centring transcendence and bathing the senses in mirage-like vistas. In the shimmering stasis of ‘Against The Tide’ choral sirens pull the ear out from shore to a 12 min standout ‘Oratorio’ surely comparable with Eno pop ambient frissons, yet shrouded with a mystery closer to Akira Rabelais’ enigmatic processes.

That grasp of atmospheric intrigue & stuff also makes for utterly sublime, tongue-tip experience in ‘Divine Light’ and thru to the tousled, Caretaker-esque crackle of ‘Threads of a Dream’, into a beatific closer ‘Higher Love’, which, if his sandman magick does its job, should be scoring your descent into the pillow or states of pure bliss.

Really exquisite stuff.

items.body:
Bursting at the seams with ideas and mushy emotionality, Cindy Lee's hypnagogic 2-hour magnum opus has quite rightly been touted as one of the best albums of the year - if not the decade. Ex-Women frontperson Patrick Flegel's vision of rock 'n roll is anachronistically nostalgic, an oily tincture of vintage psych, dilated funk and ghosted girl group pop that stews in its heartbreaking sincerity. Urgent listening for fans of Jessica Pratt, Brian Wilson, The Walker Brothers, U.S. Girls or Karen Carpenter.

It makes sense that Flegel launched their seventh Cindy Lee full-length on their web 1.0-style Geocities homepage earlier this year. The long-running web hosting service holds a special place in the hearts for people of a certain age - it's not so much what it was, exactly, but what it represented at a time when the implications of a digital future weren't yet clear. 'Diamond Jubilee' arrives at a time when nostalgia has been not just hyper-commodified, but weaponised; the concept of looking back to a time when life was easier, safer and simpler is intertwined with the acceleration of technological progress. Before we were made aware of the deluge of information that surrounded us, culture was very different - messages were easier to parse, and criticism, rightly or wrongly, was far more universally accepted. Flegel assaults us with content here - the album weighs in at 32 tracks - and although they repeatedly draw from the past, their yesteryear isn't fixed, or particularly physical. Their nostalgia is purposefully fantastical, a reverb-drenched collage of ideas that spans the long history of rock 'n roll and radio pop, and buried in amongst the tangled artifice is a strain of emotional earnestness that's refreshingly rare. 

None of this will be a huge surprise to anyone who's familiar with Flegel's prior Cindy Lee canon or their work with Women - one of the most quietly influential Canadian art rock bands of the '00s. But 'Diamond Jubilee', despite its length, focuses their gaze, subverting and twisting rock's litany of stereotypes until its impressionistic spatter of half-remembered aesthetics coagulates into an anxiously contemporary statement. There's the muddy echo of West African pop in the guitar phrasing that underpins the title track, before disco-era strings and boxy West Coast psych drums interrupt the mood abruptly; and it's Flegel's androgynous Brian Wilson-style cries that wring the passion out of the track. From bar to bar, the track morphs almost seamlessly, and Flegel anchors the chaos with their words. "What could I find, in a fantasy," they purr. "A burning memory, of something true." And it's not just genre that they cram into the meat grinder: on 'Baby Blue', the already lo-fi textures takes a hit when Flegel pushes the psych rock thuds into the red, transforming the kick drum into an empty pop that disappears into the fudgy, distorted guitars, and on the exotica-tinged 'Til Polarity's End', Flegel drowns the entire track in saturation so it sounds as if it's vibrating through a flooded abandoned factory.

It's an album that's craftily casual, as if you're supposed to assume it's been hastily cobbled together unless you decide to scratch at the wallpaper. There's a near-ambient quality to many of the tracks, that harnesses the same mixture of uneasy homesickness and reverie as the best vaporwave, but Flegel is consistently there to remind us that whatever it is we might be feeling, we're not isolated. "I'm only dreaming," they sing over near invisible bass twangs and kosmische arpeggios on 'Always Dreaming'. "Things aren't as awful as they're seeming." Even on the more formal pop moments - like 'Kingdom Come' or the heartbreaking 'If You Hear Me Crying' - Flegel's girl group swing is disrupted by their diaphanous reverb, peculiar tunings and odd rhythms. A chirpy, echoing beat patters over the former, while Flegel adds wonky strums and coarse, unexpected noises, singing "I could have sworn I heard you call my name, over the melodies of yesterday," as if pulling flesh from bone, and revealing the album's circulatory system.

It's an album that sticks in the throat, a set of broadly hypnogogic pop vignettes that embrace the expected cultural nihilism, but also grasping the passion that defined another era. "All I've got's this song," they cry on 'Don't Tell Me I'm Wrong'. "And your memory."

items.body:
Effortlessly easy on the ear and yet still somehow fathoms-deep, Tara Clerkin Trio’s latest is their most refined and fully-formed transmission yet, mining a precious sweetspot between chamber-jazz, Plone-style bric-a-brac electronics, Crescent’s lo-fi reveries and the urban pressure of the Young Echo collective, unpicking decades of British musical history in the process. Trust, it’s a special one.

Like every great band, TCT know their history. They've grown up with and formed their identity in the shadow of Bristol's musical lore, whether it's The Pop Group, Massive Attack or Flying Saucer Attack, and when they use traceable elements, it feels like a believable part of their DNA. Thankfully, they meaningfully add to that narrative too, not adapting an aesthetic for easy consumption. Part of this might be down to their makeup; they formed in the late 20-teens from the ashes of the Tara Clerkin Band, a larger ensemble that Clerkin had put together to expand the scope of her folk-y pop compositions. And when most of the members moved on, stepbrothers Sunny-Joe Paradiso and Patrick Benjamin stuck around to see where the road might lead. All "proper" players, they've traditionally let their songs appear from what sounds like loose, casual improvisations, like you're tuned into Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society' band running through Laika's 'Silver Apples of the Moon'.

So you get a song like the brilliant 'Ups & Downs', that simmers for a good four minutes with wheezing harmonium, double bass and clarinet, percussion just rumbling in the background somewhere, before a jerky sampled beat, Mellotron strings and Clerkin's voice would have you thinking Matt Elliott's behind the boards. But 'Somewhere Good' is also remarkably tight when it needs to be, walking a tightrope between easy breezy and meticulous with acrobatic skill. Opener 'Lake Walk', for example, sounds intentionally naive, jammed out loosely on synthesised and real woodwind that's caught in a vortex of Space Echo, before 'Lazy Daisy' cuts it short with its more ordered (but still kinda slouchy) beat-heavy dreampop atmosphere. It's where the album's shape really coagulates, between Broadcast's dramatic early EPs (back when they were touring with Plone) and Pram's best shit, just lightly tweezed at the edges, its creases relaxed to fit in with Laila Sakini's quietly genius 'Paloma'. And that mood carries the record even when Clerkin's voice - pursed into a soulful croon or a lackadaisical murmur - vanishes completely. One of the most gripping moments arrives with 'There Was a Nice Sunset', effortlessly matching slowcore drums with piano flourishes and synths, locking into the same general feeling but widening the boundaries, nodding to Adrian Sherwood's lysergic work on Creation Rebel's 'Starship Africa'. 

There's years of British musical history baked into this stuff, and yet it feels wholly new.

items.body:
Of all Jan Jelinek’s formidable output, this album has always been the one for us. More resolved and driven than 'Loop-Finding Jazz Records' (which appeared two years later), less reliant on glitch than Farben, it was essentially Jelinek's most satisfying and complete prototype for a new kind of sample-based music deeply immersed in the spirit of Jazz, without making any direct reference to it. 

Originally released via Move D’s Source imprint back in 1999, 'Personal Rock' is situated somewhere between 'Loop-Finding Jazz Records', his Farben output, and Move D's Conjoint work, full of subtle production flourishes sliding around deep House structures that belong to pre-millenial IDM, but which transcend its overly-fussy, masculine templates.

The music is brooding and full of romance, designed for late night immersion and bolstered by what we reckon is the most forward thinking and timeless production of Jelinek’s output over the last two decades. Impossible to pull highlights, it’s an album best experienced from end-to-end through multiple listens, drawing you into its quietly euphoric, blue mood.

items.body:
One of those releases that makes you feel like no other music exists for a hot minute, Dean Blunt returns with a second Black Metal album for Rough Trade, delving deeper into his unfathomable yet completely approachable and direct take on visceral x melancholic folk-pop. Spoiler: It’s really fucking good.

Aided on most of the songs here by Joanne Robertson’s vocal counterpoint and Giles Kwakeulati King-Ashong’s skittering drums, these songs once again connect to AR Kane’s distinct approach to the avant grade thru imperfection. In effect, it feels like Blunt manages to squeeze all the sterile sheen out of overly tasteful music, leaving a throbbing mass of flesh, blood vessels, nerve endings - exposed and beautiful. It’s what AR Kane called ‘Kaning’ (see Dhanveer Singh Brar’s excellent 'Beefy's Tune’ book for more on this) - and effectively provides a vital riposte to a world in which so much “art" is presented and consumed as a form of numbing.

And that riposte requires no explanation - a personal narative woven with little concession to anything - there’s not even a tracklisting or credits on the physical formats, instead Blunt’s ideas are wrapped up in a succession of first grade earworms, string sections here and there, billowing subs - all melancholy, blunt smoke and bliss. 

"Flaws are discontinuities that act as tiny fissures, allowing the dim and distant, diffused gem light of pre-creation to slip thru - it is this that music existed for - a signpost, a reminder, a note.” Rudy Tambala / A.R. Kane

Black Metal 2 is as real as it gets.

items.body:
Among our most loved ‘90s ambient house records, Terre Thaemlitz’s debut album is mercifully - finally - expanded and reissued for its 30th anniversary, including an incredible prototype for ambient Memphis rap instrumentals and some would even say dubstep - now expanded to well over two hours long, with a delectable bonus disc full of deep cuts.

One that puts a lump in our throat from the opening strokes, ‘Tranquillizer’ marks a key point of departure for Thaemlitz from the deep house they DJ’d at NYC clubs from the late ‘80s to fully embrace its spiritual descendants - ambient house and downbeat - and embark on a stellar oeuvre defined by a timeless sound sensitivity and pathos. 

The original version of Thaemlitz’s maiden album voyage would include ‘Raw Through a Straw’ - a sublime 11 minute transition from new age synth blooz to rollin breaks - alongside seven other cuts that beautifully took the potential of a broader canvas to paint widescreen visions of post-club music at the ’90’s midriff. This reissue now expands the 69 minute OG to over twice the length with never-before-heard, raw, alternate versions and inclusions of related, contemporaneous material from the same era.

Effectively picking up the baton from the likes of the KLF or The Orb and L.B. Bad’s new age house, and with uncanny parallels here and there to Move D and Jonah Sharp’s Reagenz project of the same era, on ‘Tranquilizer’ Thaemlitz would delineate and diffuse deep house’s romantic energies and spirit along electro-acoustic and sanguine vectors with a dreamlike seduction and melancholic traction that resonates with listeners’ needs into the present day. His perfectly slanted opener ’040468’ is titled for the date of MLK’s death (and coincidentally the year of Terre’s birth) and is a massive percy for us, spending over 8 minutes layering radio interceptions and shine-eyed synths into a lather, underlined by an LFO-flared sub-bassline with a gait that surely parallels the humid lean of early Memphis rap instrumentals (just down the road from her formative Missouri) or G-funk, and most uncannily pre-echoes the halfstep and meditative minimalism of early dubstep by a decade. A longtime travelling partner for us, it definitely warrants the cost of admission alone - it’s that good.

The rest of the OG follows to limn the sort of curious magick Thaemlitz would expand on in later years, with the ambient blues of ‘Fat Chair’ like a solemn echo of The Orb, and ‘Meditation of the Mountain Oyster’ rolling out tabla breaks into acidic horizons, and the closing section of melt-on-mind downbeats in ‘Hovering Glows’ thru the concrète-ambient frissons of ‘2 A.M. On a Silo’ to ‘Fina/Departure’ frankly leaving us in a puddle of tears and feels. The bonus disc is also totally prime, threading reverb-contrails thru ‘Get in and Drive’, an unmissable reminder of her deep house roots, two previously unreleased edits of ‘Fina’, and a stunning version of the spine-kissing ‘Hovering Glows’, plus its subtly re-tuned ‘Little Guy Mix’.

For us, ‘Tranquillizer’ is an epitome of ambient music as deeply affective, dematerialised soul music, we can only hope others will get as much from this reissued prompt as we have over the years - an indelibly imprinted carousel of memories, fond and forlorn. 

please remember that we support Terre and Comatonse Recordings' efforts to keep projects offline, minor, and acting queerly. When purchasing this item, we ask you to refrain from uploading and indiscriminate sharing in any form. <3

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi's kraut-techno-free jazz magnum opus is back for its 10th anniversary -  an ambitious ensemble piece featuring an all-star list of players including Ricardo Villalobos, Keith Fullerton Whitman, Mark Fell, crys Cole, Will Guthrie, Arto Lindsay and Konrad Sprenger... Wooooo

You've got to admire Ambarchi's chutzpah here. 'Hubris' is an all you can eat buffet of his various musical cravings, a chance for his friends, influences and collaborators to flex a little and for Ambarchi to attempt to ride the groove like an experienced cowboy on an out-of-control bucking bronco. The first side is the biggest surprise, a dedication to Wang Chung's enduring, disco-influenced 'To Live and Die in L.A.' soundtrack that begins with ping-ponging guitar notes and Jim O'Rourke's synth blips, before elusive Berlin-based composer Konrad Sprenger (aka Joerg Hiller) drops in with some motorized guitar vamps. It's rhythmic gear that fits in with the Berlin school until Mark Fell appears in the final third with some typically fractured percussion.

On the flip, the groove loosens after a short guitar interlude. Ricardo Villalobos takes over with a suitably winding, minimal throb over live rhythms played by Joe Talia and Will Guthrie simultaneously as krautrock techno mutates into disco fusion. Keith Fullerton Whitman tries to nudge the track off the rails with his modular expositions, but the path is set - Arto Lindsay's axe is just the icing on the cake. By the end of the side, we're in full jazz-noise mode: everything's still pegged to Villalobos' central pulse, but that's the only element that's bolted down. 

Hard to believe it's 10 years already - we can't think of a better skeleton key to unlock the secrets behind Black Truffle's musical identity.

items.body:
'Force Majeure' looks back on ACR's P-Funk-inspired fifth album 'Force' and plucks out a handful of unreleased versions of tracks from the album - including the title track that never made it to the original release.

By 1986, ACR were a very different band than when they started. Founder members Simon Topping and Peter Terrell left after finishing their fourth album, 'I'd Like to See You Again', forcing the band to regroup. Bassist and vocalist Jez Kerr and guitarist/trumpeter Martin Moscrop took the reins, bringing in Kalima's Tony Quigley and retaining keyboardist Andy Connell before he left to concentrate on his popular pop project Swing Out Sister.

But despite the chaos at the time, the album's a sturdy entry in the ACM canon, a fusion of post-punk, funk and nascent electro elements that still stands out. This companion release showcases a few raw-er takes - the version of 'Naked and White' benefits from the additional saturation and mixing desk chaos - and it's a treat to hear the lounge-y title track, that's for sure.

items.body:
Reworked from the original 'Sextet' session recordings by Bizarre Inc's Andrew Meecham (aka The Emperor Machine), 'The Joy of Sextet' celebrates the art-funk landmark's 45th anniversary without having to drudge up an extra disc of demos.

Anniversary reissues are just a part of life right now; pick a round number and you can guarantee some label or other is putting together a special remastered edition. And that's why 'The Joy of Sextet' is so novel - there's some elbow grease gone into it, with Meecham going back to the original recordings and putting his own spin on the entire record.

He's not completely off track, either; it's a suite of versions that's a little more dynamic than a simple remaster. Meecham adds "some new dynamics", imparting his contemporary engineering smarts on material that was recorded in Stockport way back in 1981. It's never sounded better: disco-inspired opener 'Lucinda' smacks and lurches, pumping very differently but giving plenty of space for Martha Tilson's casually affecting vocals, while the lengthy 'Knife Slits Water' has been fleshed out with watery textures and even more mind-bending FX. It's subtle, but it works.

items.body:
Curated by Rosa Pistola, 'Dioses Tribales' surveys Mexico's tribal landscape, placing scene architects like Javier Estrada, Ricardo Reyna, DJ Mouse, DJ Tetris and Dj Morphius alongside beatmakers who are steering its current course, such as "TEKTRIBAL" innovator Freebot and Monterrey's Clap Freckles.

Pistola continues her "Tribal Sound System" project with this tight, tidy selection; rewind a few weeks and you'll remember 'Incorrigible', her latest album that built a sequence of rickety, hard-swung club tracks on the foundations of Mexico's tribal sound. 'Dioses Tribales' is a companion piece in a sense, providing a way for Pistola to pay her respects to the scene's pioneers and also highlight her contemporary peers - basically, it's an invaluable (and very digestible) line in to a movement that's far too often misunderstood outside of Mexico. The first vibrations were felt back in the early 2000s, when producers in Monterrey and Mexico City began to define their own sound as American house and techno flooded local clubs. Back then, you could wander round any city center and hear local bands playing indigenous music on pan flutes, shakers and traditional drums. And it was Ricardo Reyna, on 2005's 'Danza Azteca', who was the first artist to integrate these elements into his forward-thinking productions. This track's the reason it was labeled tribal prehispánico music in the first place, in fact.

Fittingly, Pistola opens the compilation with three of tribal's key artists. Reyna provides a sequel to his milestone, 'Danza Azteca II (El baile de los Dioses)', a track that shows the development that's happened in the last two decades, spicing up the central 4/4 kick with vocal chants, clattering rhythms and an urgent, driving bassline. And then Pistola puts the spotlight on tribal guarachero, the sound that emerged as artists began to fold in rhythms from Cumbia and other Afro-Cuban and Afro-Spanish dances. Manu Morales, aka DJ Mouse, is one of the most conspicuous early visionaries in this respect - his sunny 2005 breakout 'Folklore' is still one of the genre's touchstones. And he appears here with another nod to the Caribbean, muddling reggaetón's ubiquitous 'Dem Bow' rhythm, repurposed from Shabba Ranks' 1991 anthem, with EDM stabs and clanking pan drums. Oaxaca's DJ Tetris, meanwhile, was responsible for shaping tribal costeño, notoriously defining the sound on that epic 'N.A.A.F.I Tribal' compilation from 2014. His 'Rumbea Conmigo' is a collaboration with DJ Giovanni Rios that shows how, in the coastal south, tribal fused with Mariachi music, using synths to replace the accordions.

And it wouldn't be proper if there wasn't an appearance from Javier Estrada. Estrada didn't invent tribal prehispánico, but you could say he perfected it - just peep his 2014 album of the same name. And that's where Pistola pulls 'Guerrero Azteca' from. It's arguably one of the genre's affecting tracks, packed out with animalistic growls, deep, pounding rhythms and ASMR-ready rainforest sounds that seem to have directly inspired Pistola's own productions. And over on German netlabel KUMBALE a year later, Alfonso Luna released his own 'TRIBAL PREHISPANICO' treatise, referencing its potent cocktail of percussive dings and vocal snippets with the brilliant 'Bakalao'. The contemporary charge then is led by Pistola's production partner FREEBOT who displays how modern techniques have shaped his razor-sharp, Berghain-ready "TEKTRIBAL" sound on 'Ela toma (Dioses tribales)' and Clap Freckles, who made his name producing cheeky bootlegs and edits, and impresses with his hypnotic exclusive 'Los Dioses Tribales (Deja fluir)'.

We can't think of a better way to get acquainted with tribal's past, present and future - even the cover, showing the genre's notorious pointed boots, is iconic. You know what to do.

items.body:
Cooper Crain, Dan Quinlivan and Rob Frye extend the 'Inland See' universe with two sides of additional tweaks and edits, adding field recordings, autoharp and kalimba to their analog synth vamps and motorik rhythms.

If you tuned into their last album, an ecstatic, Cluster-inspired romp that sprayed whipped cream over Bitchin Bajas usual proggy selection of exotic oscillations, then 'Isle Peaks' will play like a fitting sequel. It's not a remix record, but the source material was pulled from the same electric sessions, where stems were re-examined, edited and tweaked and new elements were added to build out the "Bajas cinematic universe," in their own words. On the first side, 'Ajami' evolves its pinging kalimba sequence with brassy analog exaltations, bringing in the horn only when necessary before the track explodes into a post-Stereolab firework display of squelchy synths, two note basslines and distorted leads.

On the title track, crickets sing in the background while the trio build up their atmosphere from reverberating autoharp textures that they layer into Laraaji-like cascades of ambient bliss - only tipping into Berlin school kosmische biz in the final act.

items.body:
The latest from A Colourful Storm’s Fleetway Tapes sublabel comes from Tokyo-based selector, composer and NTS resident Abiu, mining an hour of mostly Japanese prog, no wave and avant-industrial nuggets, floating into spoken word, free jazz and fringe dubs that’ll make you wonder where the hell she finds her tunes. If you've chewed up the Concentric Circles mixes on Berceuse Heroique and exhausted Blackest Ever Black’s ‘Id Mud’ mixtape series - this one’s for you.

One of those tapes you have to sink deep into rather than a casual dip, 'It's the Rest of a Stump' is packed to the gills with unclassifiable fire - avant oddities that are far too deep for any algorithm. Abiu will be a familiar name if you've scraped around the edges of the NTS schedule where her regular transmissions betray her vast knowledge; a show where you can find lesser-known art rock next to scrappy outsider techno, EBM and synthwave, Japanese folk sandwiched between spoken word and modern jazz sides. How she finds any of it, we're not sure, but it's the kind of gear that will inevitably lead to lengthy Discogs sessions - we guarantee it. 

So she's a lifer, for sure. And that's exactly the kind of feeling you get when you sit through this one. There's no need to go track to track because the individual elements aren't really why it works - it's the expedition that Abiu takes you on, harking back to a time when digging hadn't been so sanitised by bait algorithms and “released on this day xx years ago” campaigns. For an hour, we're dropped into a musty back room leafing through used bins and racks of tapes, searching through newsgroups and blogs - finding loose threads and wormholes and following them to albums that are prob 95% shit with just a few short minutes of glory buried inside. Abiu's done the work for us basically.

And if you want some added credentials, Abiu is also a researcher at Saidera Ai Design, the acoustics wing of Saidera Mastering, the team that just restored and remastered Miles Davis's catalog. 

Whewwww!

items.body:
French cold wave and goth disco par excellence. Not hard to imagine Annie Hogan spinning the likes of ‘L’Appel Du Froid’ at The Batcave, or insouciant, kohl-eyed Gallic teens bopping at their local goth jamboree to this lot. Evidently there’s clear reasons why this DIY self-release of ’88 now trades for triple figures on resale markets…

“Opéra de Nuit emerge from their long slumber to grace Dark Entries with the frostiest of reissues. Formed in 1982 in Valréas in the southeast of France, Opéra de Nuit only released 3 records throughout their career: EPs in 1984 and 1986, with a full LP following in 1988. But devotees of dark music will need no introduction to this band, who are almost definitional of the coldwave genre, and whose rabid cult following has each record readily trading for three-digit prices. Opéra de Nuit’s sound is pure hellish heaven: frigid synths, jangly guitars, and sorrow-laden vox. 

Check out the pummelling desperation of “Annabella,” the uber-brooding vibes of “Boris Transylvania Camp,” or the elegant anthem “Karen Lloyd” (and don’t forget to watch the video!). This reissue collects their entire newly remastered discography – thirteen lucky tracks. This reissue marks the first time that their work will be reissued on vinyl and digital, and is presented in gatefold jacket with lyrics and photos. Whether you’re new to the genre or a veteran of the coldest waves, Opéra de Nuit brings the essential sound of immortal despair.”

items.body:
FELT capture deep & mysterious activities for posterity with a double bill from someone called bushes (no clues!) and scene veteran Klaus, recorded and mixed by Murray Collier (aka Dip Friso, Grim Lusk) in Glasgow, 2024. Trust there’s oodles of intrigue & stuff inside.

Always encouraging when music has no immediate frames of reference, RIYL’s or FFO’s, and this lot do it very fucking well, operating at a sort of eyes-at-half-mast tempo and headspace that’s neither ambient nor primed for the club, like some kinda holding music between modes of existence (we didn’t say liminal lol), full of dank atmosphere and the promise of whatever the night has in store. 

If the A side gives a whiff of isolation, the flip is all dusk and romance, snatches of saxophone drifting off in the distance with bass pulses and endless delay sending us to an unintelligible, beautiful place.

One of those tapes we guarantee you’ll rinse endlessly, we’ve had it on a loop for a couple of hours and trust it casts a fucking spell.

items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."

items.body:
Layered guitars, synths and wordless vocals set the scene on the introspective solo debut by Lynn Wright.

"Wright, who has mostly eschewed developing a fixed artistic identity throughout his already long career, has preferred to remain on the periphery of collaborative projects and behind the scenes. It took until recent times for him to make “Before The Sinking Plains”, which arrives as his first solo recording after decades of traversing underground scenes in New York and beyond. Wright defines the album as “a collection of atmospheric compositions structured as songs or songs masking as atmospheric compositions.”

The album began during a long neurological illness as guitar loops Wright would make each morning in his apartment and let play quietly in the background. At some point he began recording the ones he liked and adding layers of treated guitars, vocals, and synths, and then, eventually, giving them defined structures. The album features none of the aggression of his louder bands and improvisatory projects, but retains the dark hues.

Before The Sinking Plains lives on the familiar peripheries of our post-everything sound world, with elements of everything from washed-out dream pop and atmospheric drone works to sparse noir folk and minimalist vocal composition moving within the linings of Wright's subtle yet grand pieces, creating a perfect backdrop for watching the sky merge with the vast open fields.

Since relocating to Berlin some years ago from New York, he has worked closely with composer Simon Goff, who mixed his current album, as an editor, engineer and composer on various film and recording projects. He also plays lap steel guitar in Swans bassist Dana Schechter’s band Insect Ark. This is just the top of the iceberg when it comes to Wright's collaborations and projects throughout the years."

items.body:
I can feel the waves is Frances Chang's debut on RVNG Intl.

"A boundary-pushing musician and multi-media artist from Brooklyn, New York, Frances Chang disrupts accepted reality through her unique and enchanting compositions. Chang’s songs are an exercise in communication, probing the tension between idiosyncratic personal experience and the drive to understand, and be understood, through a collective language.

For “I can feel the waves,” a piano-centric melody is ornamented with primitive electronics and poetic vocals. The track boldly demonstrates Chang’s strength for unconventional yet contagious songwriting, and pioneers a genre the artist refers to as “slacker prog”: roomy and playful, offbeat and occasionally jarring, brimming with spiritual and emotional resonance.

The b-side, “Marry,” is a rollicking yet laid-back composition, with undaunted wobbly kicks bubbling under pianistic textures until a dialogue, acted out between Chang and Sylvia Gorelick, takes the foreground in the final moments of the track. As the instrumental carries its freewheeling pulse forward, the conversation, inspired by films like Kenneth Lonergan’s Margaret and Catherine Breillat’s Fat Girl!, along with Broken Social Scene’s “Anthems for a Seventeen-Year Old Girl,” turns toward the relationship between internal subjectivity and the external necessity of “staying small.”

Where is Frances headed from here? A piano is at the center, synths and strings swelling around its shoulders. A little less tension, a lot more production. Some shadows will be encountered, some forgotten skeletons unearthed. Music excavated from the subtler, deeper layers of cerebral and shared experiences. Music that is truly its own."

items.body:
Suzanne Ciani’s ‘gay male’ alter ego Steve with a 1982 foray into peak time wavey business, including that coca cola bottle opening sound she did the sound design for plus a pitched down vocal from Ciani and a cameo from Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream, followed by a killer slice of filtered House  ‘Steve Saves the World’ and a crazy, ‘Home Of The Brave’ style linndrum closer “Steve Happy Birthday Wishes”. Crazy find!

"Legendary composer, sound designer, and Buchla maestra Suzanne Ciani has a staggering list of accolades and accomplishments, from scoring Hollywood films to releasing influential new age records to literally designing the Coca-Cola bottle-opening sound. In the late 70s/early 80s, Ciani, while living in New York, acquired an Eventide H 949 harmonizer, which offered high fidelity pitch-shifting. In her words, “When I adjusted the pitch of my voice to 0.80, my natural voice became re-invented as what was clearly a gay man, who I called Steve. I became Steve; and Steve expressed himself as only he could.” Ciani adopted the male persona and collaborated with Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream on “Steve Goes to a Party.” The track features Ciani-as-Steve adlibbing in decadent and delirious fashion alongside Baumann’s robotically funky beats.

Steve would emerge again a few years later at George Louvis’s Stardust Studios in New Jersey, to create “Steve Saves the World,” an absurdist and ecstatic proto-house groover complete with a gospel-esque chorus from the Stardust All-Stars. This EP is rounded out by a birthday wish to Ciani’s then-boyfriend Alfred on “Steve Happy Birthday Wishes” featuring Suzanne. Steve’s Out of the Closet perfectly captures the delirious techno-poptimism of the 1980s downtown avant-garde, with parallels in Robert Ashley’s Perfect Lives or Lynn Goldsmith’s project Will Powers, responsible for the track “Adventures in Success.” The Steve sleeve was designed by Eloise Shir-Juen Leigh, and the record also includes a birthday card with liner notes from Ciani."

items.body:
New LP from Ty Segall + full band (Ben Boye/Evan Burrows/Mikal Cronin/Emmett Kelly).

"In the spring of 2025, right around the release of Possession, Ty Segall started hearing voices, calmly at first, but soon screaming: “Get the band back together!!!” - immediately, his mind began working, creating, collecting and collating riffs for songs, an album that he and the band — Ben Boye, Evan Burrows, Mikal Cronin & Emmett Kelly — will come to all call Chrome.

Chrome — the element, not the album — is shiny, reflective, resistant to corrosion. Chrome the album’s got that too: in hard-springing rock strung with lyrically allusive passages moving furtive and bleak through labyrinthine paths in the darkness. Joining social phenomena and autobiographical dream imagery in song-sequenced, head-snapping flashes, hitting left/right hemispheres fast and furiously. In massive riffs and thudding power in the rhythm core, twin-guitar attack and parry, tightly arrayed lines of fuzz distortion, keyboard textures of bright and thickness. All mixed immediate and flexible, colorful and clean, spicy-sweet, with Ty’s vocals of vinegar and sand, wine and grains of silver nitrate, pointing the way. That’s Chrome.

The band came together fast and hard, their five heads writing half the songs here, with others featuring Ty and Evan collabing, Matt Yoka and Denée Segall writing some too. Accounting, we believe, for its high-performing social nature and hot rocks. Its guitars slammed immaculate, big waves & dark apocolypto energy bonfires on the beach, from proto to punk to grunch, projected from the crowd-sourced energy of their mind-meld to shake the cages of the larger collective beyond."

items.body:
Bit of a special one from John T. Gast’s 5 Gate Temple, finding anomalous wildcard St Agnis with a set of classical guitar improvisations under the Victoria Mingot alias - all enchantingly loose-limbed lowercase strums and murmurs tipped for fans of Loren Connors, Graham Lambkin, Virginia Astley, Vincent Gallo, Klein.

‘God Spill’ runs like a diary of broken sleep, taking things to their quietest, most ruminative depths. The dozen pieces are defined by plaintive melodic structuring for classical guitar, voice and pedals, on what sounds like dictaphone recordings that imbue everything with an eerie ferric intimacy. And those vocals are pretty special when they do appear, like a flickering filament in the aether of ‘i saw the sign’, recalling Mary Maddox off Mike Ratledge’s ‘Riddles of the Sphinx’, floating, Virginia Astley-like, on the frayed Lambkin-esque strum of ‘in plentitude of the harvest’, or more textural in the mournful raga meditation ‘om dhyana’.

The exquisitely discreet balance of un-showy yet transfixing instrumental economy is magnified by an un-moored sense of time and place and what the label call “soft rage” -  fully revealing itself with repeat listens.

Special stuff.

Jubilant art-funk about cocaine addiction—absolutely. Swooning orchestral pop about Jerry Garcia—why not? items.body:
Asher White releases latest album "Love Aggregates" via Joyful Noise Recordings.

"For any other artist, an album like Asher White’s Love Aggregates might come out of a conscious push to treat no idea as off-limits, to make something bold and new. Jubilant art-funk about cocaine addiction—absolutely. Swooning orchestral pop about Jerry Garcia—why not? Rippling electronic noise, jazzy brushed drums, an elderly motorcyclist with dementia, a profoundly emotional bass solo—put them all in one song. There are threadbare folk tunes, glammed-up power-pop bangers, “Sir Duke” horn charts, Morton Feldman string arrangements, layers of guitar feedback like violins made of liquid chrome. Yes, for another artist, Love Aggregates might be the most adventurous album in their catalog. For Asher White, it’s what passes for settling down.

White is 25 years old and has been making records—writing, recording, producing, and playing almost everything herself—for over a decade. She’d released two dozen of them on Bandcamp before catching the indie-rock industry’s attention with 2024’s Home Constellation Study and last year’s 8 Tips for Full Catastrophe Living. The latter album’s dizzy eclecticism and formidable craft landed her on Rolling Stone’s Future 25 list with the likes of xaviersobased and Oklou, along with a slew of other accolades. That came as something of a surprise to White, who didn’t craft the chaotic 8 Tips with a breakthrough in mind. Love Aggregates feels like a chance, for one of the most thrilling musical talents of her generation, at a more deliberate introduction.

She wrote and recorded her new album while her previous one was gathering momentum, tinkering in the DIY recording studio where she always works, acutely conscious now that people would be listening to whatever she came up with. At around the same time, her years-long romantic relationship ended in a flurry of betrayal and addiction, her first experience of devastating heartbreak. Even so, Love Aggregates is not a bitter album about wallowing or seething, but instead making use of those impulses as raw materials in work that transcends the specificity of its origins, fashioning them into something surprising and new."

items.body:
Up until the release of his debut album in 2014, Shinichi Atobe managed to stay off grid since his release on Basic Channel’s Chain Reaction imprint back in 2001. He delivered the second-to-last 12” on the label and then disappeared without a trace, leaving behind a solitary 12” and a trail of speculation that led some people to wonder whether the project was in fact the work of someone on the Basic Channel payroll.

That killer Chain Reaction 12” was also a long time favourite of Demdike Stare, who had been trying to follow the trail and make contact with Atobe for many years before a lead from the Basic Channel office turned up an address in japan and - unbelievably - an album full of archival and new material. That material was compiled and released back in 2014 as Butterfly Effect.

And what a weird and brilliant album it is - deployed with a slow-churn opener that sounds like a syruppy Actress track, before working through a brilliantly sharp and tactile 9 minute Piano House roller that sounds like DJ Sprinkles at his most bittersweet, before diving headlong into a heady, Vainqueur inspired droneworld. It’s full of odd little signatures that gives the whole thing a timeless feel - like a sound bubble from another era.

items.body:
Wah Wah Wino​'s Davy Kehoe, Morgan Buckley and Olmo are joined by avant legend Roger Doyle, among others, on a delectably brilliant, 54 minute collage, re-upped with new artwork for 2026.

An ode to the putative pleasures of ketamine, ‘KWALK’ emulates the effect of everyone’s fave equine dissociative with a mazy disarray of folk rock, ambient electronics and balmy, bandy-legged grooves bent for getting ketty with it. Inside, song structures quiesce to smeared samples and fractal lines of thought perhaps familiar to anyone who’s done a bump or two.

As with all Wino joints, normal logic is out the window, replaced by a loosey goosey slant that's a real pleasure to follow. In their slippery snakes ’n ladders chicanery, ‘KWALK’ recalls everything from Davy Kehoe's endlessly-rinsed 'Storm Desmond' to the Lost Highway OST, The KLF’s 'Chill Out' to Sigtryggur Berg Sigmarsson & BJ NIlsen’s ‘Avantgardegasse’ ace thru to Don Cherry’s communal free jazz jams and Laura Cannell’s folk flights in our minds, and should be considered a go-to slab for those times when the sofa’s on the ceiling and everyone’s too munted to pick another tune.

We have a special place in our hearts for mixtapes/collage pieces pressed to vinyl - and this one is prob the best we've heard since John T. Gast's 'Invocations II' set for Blowing Up The Workshop a few years back.

items.body:
An iconic album originally brought to life via Sweden's peerless iDEAL Recordings, Kali Malone’s 'The Sacrificial Code’ is a major work featuring almost two hours of concentrated, creeping organ pieces aligned to non traditional intonation/tuning systems. It's a stunning realisation of ideas borne out of academic and conceptual rigour, with a perception-altering quality that encourages exploration without a preordained endpoint.

The Sacrificial Code’ takes a more surgical approach to the methods first explored on last year’s ‘Organ Dirges 2016 - 2017’. Over the course of three parts performed on three different organs, Malone’s minimalist process captures a jarring precision of closeness, both on the level of the materiality of the sounds and on the level of composition.The recordings here involved careful close miking of the pipe organ in such a way as to eliminate environmental identifiers as far as possible - essentially removing the large hall reverb so inextricably linked to the instrument. The pieces were then further compositionally stripped of gestural adornments and spontaneous expressive impulse -  an approach that flows against the grain of the prevailing musical hegemony, where sound is so often manipulated, and composition often steeped in self indulgence. It echoes Steve Reich’s sentiment “..by voluntarily giving up the freedom to do whatever momentarily comes to mind, we are, as a result, free of all that momentarily comes to mind.”

With its slow, purified and seemingly austere qualities ‘The Sacrificial Code’ guides us through an almost trance-inducing process where we become vulnerable receptors for every slight movement, where every miniature shift in sound becomes magnified through stillness. As such, it’s a uniquely satisfying exercise in transcendence through self restraint and by this point inarguably a modern classic.

items.body:
Demdike Stare’s DDS label kicks off a new series of limited edition 12”s with the return of Shinichi Atobe, offering a slow evolution of his inimitable deep house, finely balanced with a new found sub-heavy bias while unlocking extra space in the upper registers.

Atobe’s third 12” since debuting on Chain Reaction in 2001 marks a subtle but crucial development of his style, leaning towards classically deep, dub house templates, assisted by additional editing and mixing from Miles ov Demdike Stare. On both sides he adds supple flesh and hypnotic emotive pathos to his stripped formula, resulting in some of the most immediate and enduring work in his canon thus far. It coincidentally also marks a decade since he first graced DDS with his debut album ‘Butterfly Effect’, followed by a tranche of cultishly acclaimed albums in the years since.

On the A-side pearl ‘Ongaku 1’ he steps out with a shimmering take on the effortless gait of M-Series blueprints, as derived from the deepest NYC house, delicately ornamented with cascading levels of detail. Precision-tooled kicks precipitate Prescription-via-Maurizio feathered dub chords, interlaced with a frisson of darker strings and synth melodies for the full goosebump. ‘Dub 6(six)’ on the flip whisks up a psychedelic lattice of arps and synth voices with ruder bass ballast, taking its sweet time before the kicks come to swing the ‘floor deep and wide. 

Straight bullets, no messing.

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items.body:
St Circul's debut album "Ley Lines" via Archaic Vaults.

"Concise collection of folkloric grime instrumentals to rise from a new moniker taken on by the elusive First Circle. A breadcrumb trail of effortlessly crafted early 2000s-era grime, trap and drill instrumentals can be found on a fairly sparse Soundcloud account and numerous NTS shows spanning the last ten years, on which he is known to play almost entirely his own material. Now a different energy takes hold on »Ley Lines«: ten tracks by the enigmatic producer to be released both on a label and in physical format for the first time.

»Ley Lines« was born from a meandering quest through South London’s more leafy dwellings. These cherished regions became a place of refuge in which to ruminate on the hopes that love and community can outlast the dwindling state of Britain’s social and political climate. Photo documentation was made which would later form the genesis for each track, and a return to the studio resulted in something which could not be fitted into the existing First Circle discography.

Harpsichord and brass samples (»A Plan Is Formed«, »Hilly Fields«) are underpinned by murky bass loops and tight militaristic percussion – motifs recognisable amongst white label grime’s most influential producers (Wiley, Skepta, Lewi White etc.) that push the formula into far more rapturous territories than any of FC’s previous productions. The more introspective moments of the album (»Wares at the Ivy House«, »Blythe Vision«) put local field recordings and devotional reverberant ambience to the forefront, alluding to St Circul’s proto-dungeon synth influences and giving the whole album a unique world all its own.

Archaic Vaults is proud to host an album which shares intrinsic roots with the label’s own South London birthplace. »Ley Lines«’ ten tracks of psychogeographic drifting are available in digital and limited cassette format via Archaic Vaults.

Mastered by Owen Pratt Design by Severin Black Artwork image by St Circul"

items.body:
Last spotted on A Good Year's 'Play', Texas-born singer, producer and multi-instrumentalist Riya Mahesh, aka Quiet Light, turns in the sequel to 2023's 'Blue Angel Sparkling Silver', mashing Imogen Heap's experimentation with The Postal Service's emo-friendly electro-pop.

There's a polish to 'Blue Angel Sparkling Silver 2', but Mahesh's production smarts don't ever overwhelm the music's emotional core. And although she plays fast and loose with the vocal effects, chopping, processing and layering her voice in much the same way Heap did when she inadvertently kickstarted cloud rap, it's still possibly to sense the human in the machine. It's a technique that's helped Mahesh get noticed recently; she appeared alongside Late Verlane on A Good Year's sublime album opener 'Dealerz' and the new mixtape sees her move to True Panther, labelmates with artists who share the same DNA: Glasser, Oklou and Lauren Auder, for example.

On 'Berlin', that seems as if it would be self-explanatory, she avoids the temptation to drape her song in techno finery, instead telling her story of over-indulgence with restraint, singing almost unaccompanied until her sparse drones are met by a simple breakbeat. Her voice is left to do the heavy lifting and it's up for the job; Mahesh is a gifted producer, sure, but as a singer she's able to really show her range, comfortably belting out power pop or existing in a more ambient space, like on 'New Dream'. She's even able to bridge the gap between electro pop and Surf Gang-style Soundcloud rap on 'Postinternetfame' - and the breathy 'New Girls' sounds like it was at least partially inspired by Burial. Nae bad at all.

items.body:
Erykah Badu teases her first album in 16 years with a collaboration with superproducer 'The Alchemist' that's as vital as anything on her 'New Amerykah' records - and far more psychoactive.

Badu just doesn't do things by half. She waits until we're ready and somehow always has the perfect sound for the moment - just think about the impact of 'Baduizm' in 1997, or the fanged 'New Amerykah: Part One (4th World War)', released on the cusp of the Obama era. 'Witch Doctor' is a lucid reflection on the media's stranglehold that Badu coaxes into a lilting, soulful coo at first, harking back to her Motown era with The Alchemist's cool-headed, jazzy keys and blunted beats. 

But there's something just beneath the surface; when the boom-bap smack fades to silence, Badu's doubletime syncopated rhythm emerges that had been driving the track all along. Badu lets it run out, dubbing out voices and loose percussive elements to enhance the syrupy, ritualistic qualities until that's the core focus of the track. Remarkable stuff, really - bring on the album.

items.body:
Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.

items.body:
Hakushi Hasegawa’s Honest Feeling Album is the Tokyo-based composer, producer and multi-instrumentalist’s second full-length release for Brainfeeder.

"Working with HaHa & The Hairpins as a backing band, Hasegawa brings greater scale and momentum to their restless blend of jazz, pop, J-rock and electronic experimentation.

Featuring collaborations with tofubeats, Lang Lee, Tsukino Mito and Accorinrin of Otoboke Beaver, the album moves between intricate arrangements, melodic songwriting and sudden shifts in pace. Lead track ‘The Owner of Sweetness’ sets the tone: a sweeping ballad where virtuosic playing and detailed production meet head-on.

For fans of Iglooghost, A. G. Cook, Yaeji, Underscores and Louis Cole."

items.body:
Jospehine Foster's 2016 release "No More Lamps In the Morning" available again via Fire Records.

"Foster, on nylon string guitar, and husband Victor Herrero, accompanying on Portuguese guitar, together weave intimate readings of songs spanning Foster's songwriting career including selections from recent albums "This Coming Gladness" (2008) and "I'm a Dreamer" (2013) and back to Born Heller (2004). Foster's new route is a free, chromatic music, a tuneful montana of mind--an expansive harmonic space dominated by Rif mountain on the horizon. As highwater as the music is, as broad the stylistic palette of the musicians, the music really exists in service of the lyrics. Two of the songs on No More Lamps are poems by Rudyard Kipling and James Joyce given musical settings by Foster. The rest arguably are musical settings of her own poems strengthened in a fiery crucible of guitars (and on 2 tracks Gyða Valtýsdóttir's cello) in which dissonant notes bend and quaver as wirefork embers, dying without affecting the glowing tonal fire which unites contrary forces in a Moroccan speakeasy. She and Herrero have performed, for an audience of burros, concerts of Federico Garcia Lorca poems set to music. A music of wandering and a music of roots."

items.body:
Necessary reissue of Marc Leclair’s immaculate Y2K micro-house/dub-house 12” as Akufen, dispensed by Low End Activist’s guess-again BRUK sibling to Sneaker Social Club - huge RIYL Maurizio, Studio 1, Mike Huckaby.

‘Architextures 1 -2 -3’ is a sought-after slice of hypnotic house by a noted pioneer of the micro-house movement that emerged in the late ‘90s. Its reissue arrives in the wake of a re-up for Marc Leclair’s (aka Akufen) sole solo album ‘Musique Pour 3 Femmes Enceintes’ (2005) with a strong reminder of his pivotal role in dressing house music down to fundamentals around the millennium, as deployed in Richie Hawtin mixes and praised for its exquisitely efficient, effortless, hiccuping funk.

It’s really all about the  A-side’s ‘Architexture 1’, a pendulous 127BPM roller inflected with chef’s kiss dub chords and frisky drums, on one of the smoothest, deepest basslines since ‘M5’. There’s a good reason why it’s been fetching triple figures on 2nd hand markets, so BRUK are doing the Lord’s work with this reissue, which also includes the slower, sub-heavier swivel of its Pt. 2, and more signature, strutting clip of his tight sampling tekkerz on Pt. 3.

TIP!

items.body:
For us, still the standout Short Span, ​a staggering label debut from Marija Rasa aka emer, previously seen on Stroom and here operating at the opiated levels where classic steppers dub techno x Lolina’s frayed dubs collide, all smouldering dubwise pearls tipped FFO False Aralia, Ugnė Uma, Rhythm & Sound, Sade.

Marija Rasa’s dream sequence of crawl-pace slugs sways on syrupy bass and is fully sublimated to seductive vapours. For anyone paying closer attention, ‘Fog’ clearly reprises and expands on the elusive, smoky vibes felt on her 2024 drop for Stroom and in ’25 for Chicago’s Lillerne Tapes. However her sound is notably strapped with more supple layers and perfused with a groggy spirit that really hits for night owls or those chasing trip hop dragons.

‘Fog’ operates at the speed of slowed thought with seven cuts to sink right into. For half an hour she swaddles minds in high tog textures as tracks pass-out into hazed bliss from the gentle descent into swole subs on ‘Below Altitude’, to gorgeous, spongiform bass and soul-grab chords of ‘Open’, and like Moritz Von Oswald smelting his jazz trio back to Rhythm & Sound fundamentals in ‘Nobody Speaks’. A knack for eking out organic detail is most enchanting on the interplay of aerosolised thizz and subs on ‘Room Five’, and leaves us levitating in the ssabæ-esque wooze to ‘The Evergreen Fog’ and hobbled, ghostly shape of ‘Calling’.

A modern classic of the form.

items.body:
A sought-after Dub Techno classic originally released on Berlin’s legendary Chain reaction in 2001, remastered from vinyl for this edition in 2015 by Matt Colton.

A massive personal favourite of Demdike Stare's, Shinichi Atobe's 'Ship Scope' was Chain Reaction's penultimate release in 2001 and, with the benefit of hindsight, also one of the label's most sublime offerings. Phase fwd to 2015 and DDS rightly put it back into circulation with this necessary reissue arriving in the wake of Atobe's much loved archival salvage, 'Butterfly Effect', which caused quite a ripple in late 2014.

Notable not only for its unusually dreamier tone - especially when compared with the rest of the CR#'s - but also for its happily lost-at-sea feel, connoting a deeply romantic and almost shoegazy late '90s / into-the-'00s deep techno aesthetic that would essentially become washed away with the advent and normalisation of mnml techno's pristine production values.

Quite simply, it's a must-have for followers of the romantic streak in Ross 154, Convextion and classic Chain Reaction - do not miss!

Conceived as a sonic reflection on the climate cr
items.body:
A richly metaphoric expression of worries about climate change and marine devastation, blending hydrophonic acoustic and electronic sources to spell out a sonorous, subaquatic narrative FFO Mark Jenkin film scores, Thomas Köner, AFX’s SAW II...

“After All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea (2023) and Black Clouds Above The Bows (2022), Amsterdam-based collective Wanderwelle presents the final entry of their album trilogy for Important Records (IMPREC). Conceived as a sonic reflection on the climate crisis and its devastating impact on coastal ecosystems, Ghosts Beneath The Brine (2026) addresses the mass deaths of fish, seabirds, crustaceans and countless other creatures that call these seas home, now rapidly being overfished, warming and acidifying.

Where antique cavalry trumpets played a central role on Black Clouds Above The Bows and a dying church organ shaped All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea, cymbals form the core of Ghosts Beneath The Brine. The instruments were submerged in seawater for extended periods of time and played with a bow at various stages of corrosion. As the bronze alloy gradually reacted with the saltwater, their sound transformed, becoming darker, more fragile and unstable. Over time, the metal began to sing in ghostly overtones, as if haunted by the waters that shaped it. Much like large groups of fish shimmering beneath the surface, the cymbals slowly lost their shine, both sonically and physically, as salt and time took hold.

Alongside its environmental narrative, the album draws from maritime mythology. Echoes of the sea bishop, the kraken, devil whales and sea serpents emerge throughout its soundscape. Once feared and revered, these creatures now exist only in the liminal space between folklore and memory, haunting the collective imagination like omens from a forgotten age. Through immersive textures and submerged harmonies, Wanderwelle intertwines myth and mourning, inviting listeners to drift between the real and the spectral. If humanity continues on its current course, familiar species such as sharks, oysters and even gulls may soon share the same fate as their legendary predecessors, becoming ghosts beneath the brine.”

items.body:
Decades of taut intuition feed forward into Russian Circles’ instrumental metal alloys of post-rock, hardcore, prog, and krautrock on their ninth album, recorded at local bastion Electrical Audio by Kurt Ballou (Converge, Mastodon, High on Fire)...

"Chicago-bred post metal trio Russian Circles new album Nine continues their unhurried evolution and disciplined refinement, leaning into their strengths while pushing at the boundaries of their sound. This is a band with no hit songs. No fan consensus on their best album. Just a reputation of consistency and quality that built one of the biggest heavy instrumental rock bands in the world.While they insist that their music is a confluence of broad-ranging influences, it’s fair to say that Russian Circles’ adventurous diversity has developed into a distinct and singular sound.

Although Russian Circles is now spread across the country - guitarist Mike Sullivan in Los Angeles, drummer Dave Turncrantz based in Chicago, and bassist/keyboardist Brian Cook living in Vashon Island, outside of Seattle - the band triangulate their relative positions for Nine. Its seven seismic tracks act as long-form oriented soundtracks to the trials and tragedies of life in the modern age. “The music we make is a collective process of reconciliation, navigation, and reflection upon aging both as individuals and as a creative entity. Life has created very real distances between us, but the band continues to be at the center, and this creative collaboration is a way of charting the passage of time while also giving us a reason to look to the future,” the band elaborates. Whereas earlier albums were almost playful in their traversing of territories, Nine is a document of a band that knows the lay of the land and is fortifying their dominion over the varied terrain."
