items.body:
Patricia Wolf's second Balmat album is the soundtrack to experimental filmmaker Edward Pack Davee's feature-length documentary 'Hrafnamynd', and mixes field recordings with AFX-esque lullaby themes, tape-mangled instrumental vamps and VHS-burn'd analog pads.

There's something oddly soothing about 'Hrafnamynd', and without seeing the documentary it's hard to know exactly why. Using film and digital, Davee recounts his childhood in Iceland through the volcanic island's ravens, exploring the landscape and folklore while scraping his own nostalgia. And Wolf's score attempts to mimic the surreal fusion of old and new by using her UDO Super 6, a powerful binaural analog-hybrid synth, to bring the past towards the present. "It has the ability to sound very modern," Wolf explains. "But can also sound so warm and fuzzy, like a synth from the 1970s." 

So we're treated to time-warped tracks like 'Early Memories', 'I Thought I Could Fly' and 'Hrafnaﬂing', the latter of which sounds as if it's an off-cut from Leila's 'Like Weather', and distressed, casual jams like 'Krummi's Theme' - the cue for the film's talking raven. But these are bounced against more self-consciously contemporary compositions; the glassy 'Huginn and Muninn', for example, or the balletic 'Surfing on Wind'. And the album's most generous track 'Echoes Through Time' reflects Wolf's full spectrum, distorting harmonies that settle into percussive sine chimes before disappearing into the distance.

items.body:
The Original Motion Picture Soundtrack for Crime 101 by experimental electronic musician, producer and composer Blanck Mass (She Rides Shotgun).

"Thunderous synth soundscapes are paired with nuanced character-driven themes creating a multi-faceted backdrop to the intense thriller. The Amazon MGM Studios film directed by Bart Layton is set against the sun-bleached grit of Los Angeles.

Crime 101 weaves the tale of an elusive jewel thief (Chris Hemsworth) whose string of heists along the 101 freeway have mystified police. When he eyes the score of a lifetime, his path crosses that of a disillusioned insurance broker (Halle Berry) who is facing her own crossroads. Convinced he has found a pattern, a relentless detective (Mark Ruffalo) is closing in, raising the stakes even higher. As the heist approaches, the line between hunter and hunted begins to blur, and all three are faced with life-defining choices– and the realization that there can be no turning back.

On creating the music, Power says :

“Crime 101 was an incredible movie to have the opportunity to score. At the centre of the story is, of course, the heist. However, it very quickly became apparent to me that this was not any heist movie, but more a Noir which happens to have a heist in it. The central characters and how their lives become intertwined was more important than the action, in a way. This is high-octane in parts, of course, but what really drew me to this movie was the character development. Lou, Davis and Sharon are the beating heart. I wanted to ‘be with them sonically’ throughout. Both the tender and the furious needed to be sympathetic with one another”."

items.body:
Composer-producer-musician-DJ Floating Points, aka Sam Shepherd's "Mere Mortals", his first full-length ballet score.
"Commissioned and directed by the San Francisco Ballet’s Artistic Director Tamara Rojo, with choreography by Aszure Barton and design and visuals by Hamill Industries, the ballet reimagines the story of Pandora in a fusion of myth, music and movement. Recorded with the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra for Deutsche Grammophon, the 14-track album is a potent mix of elegiac strings, apocalyptic brass and pulsing electronics. From the lyrical solo violin of Hope to the dissonance and pummelling percussion of Rage of the Gods, and the exquisite harp melody of Her Gift before the eeriness of Opening of the Jar, the score is rich in texture and effect. Orchestral music emerges from an electronic haze, mirroring the ballet’s central question: where does the human end and the machine begin?"

items.body:
Co-produced by Nosaj Thing and 'Donnie Darko' OST guy Michael Andrews, Eartheater's latest is the polar opposite of 2023's 'Powders', ditching the drug and club references and leaning into baby-on-board playlist fodder, including an Oklou feature. RIYL Dido, Dubstar, Sneaker Pimps.

It's still obviously an Eartheater record, more 'Phoenix' than 'Powders'. The album starts strong, with her robotically treated voice sounding oddly soothing next to a full orchestra on 'Eyes of a Dove'. Even the glossy, sync-ready 'Paradise Rains', the album's first single that details her buying back her childhood farm and conceiving her baby, is chewably eccentric, still bound to the same logic that made her bonkers early material so addictive.

items.body:
Revisiting their debut album '.After', Tujiko Noriko and Adrian Corker commission a suite of remixes, bringing in Koshiro Hino ov YPY, goat (JP) and KAKUHAN fame, Tashi Wada, DJ Trystero, Shojiro Nakaoka and DJ ojo to put their spin on the source material.

The original album only took Noriko and Corker a couple of days in the studio, but they wired the results to percussionist and arranger George Barton, who took it to the next level. They continue the thought on '.After Again', dishing out the stems to a carefully pruned list of collaborators - artists whose distinctive sounds only extend the original album's sonic universe. And of course it's the YPY version of the album's opening track 'Yasashii Sayonora' that'll have most of y'all chomping at the bit; Hino turns Corker and Noriko's source material to dust, time-stretching Noriko's vocal and zeroing in on the stuttering percussion and rusted turntable loops. Adding his signature jerks, he fills the track with clattering metallic clangs, twisting the voices into downsampled groans from a neighboring cyber-reality.

Tokyo's DJ Trystero opts for a different but similarly unique approach on his two reworks, the "All Frills" remix of 'Toku No Minato' and his "Naive Declension" version of the same track. On the former, he isolates almost indistinguishable elements of the original, setting the ghost traces to a typically deep, dubby groove and on the latter, creates a rugged, gear-heavy jam from the remains. It's actually Nakaoka who provides the weirdest - yet strangely most recognisable - versions, using his custom generative code to match Noriko's voice with whirring interference and warbling digital detritus.

items.body:
Regelbau chief Natal Zaks, who you may better known as Danish house talent Central, returns to his Picture alias hot on the heels of a full-length under the same moniker on his usual home, Short Span.

"This EP comes on P-TON, NMP's sub label, and is pristine dub techno with clean lines and minimal fuss. 'Faaaaaaaaa' has the right amount of swing and pop under sleek chords, 'Gaaaaaaaaaa' is less about firmware demotion and more about locking you in an endless cycle of brain cleansing thought. 'Kaaaaaaaa' is a darker world of cavernous bass and icy futurism and 'Tuuuuuuuu' nods to the best of Basic Channel. Proper dub techno that reinvents nothing but does everything exceptionally well."

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s holy trilogy of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smokey nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueuer, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state. But for us, his sound really comes into its own on ‘2’, where the opening melodica motif still sends electric shivers down the spine and opens out into the kind of sculpted, layered dub bass that spawned dubstep, and flows out into myriad, mesmerising permutations, but this time swapping out the hazy licks for a cavernous, brooding melancholy (that really matched this moody teenager’s psyche at the time) and reverberated through into the more humid, drizzly and funereal atmosphere conjured in the equally spellbinding spectral dub metaphysics of ‘3’.

So strong was the impact of these albums on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

items.body:
Lushest, subtropically-infused jazz lilt by seasoned Chicago musicians who’ve worked with SZA, Whitney, Lil Nas X and Clairo, between them - all stamped with International Anthem’s seal of approval and with the pirates of Milton Nascimiento and Herbie Hancock in its breezy air. Record of the summer..?

“album notes by Josh Terry: Imagine it’s late afternoon, you’re outside by the lake, and there’s sunlight on the water. This is the peaceful and contemplative scene that Matt Gold and Resavoir set on their collaborative LP Horizon. Across 10 lush and exploratory tracks, it’s the product of two Chicago-based musicians—Will Miller, the acclaimed trumpeter, composer, and producer who’s worked with SZA, Whitney, and more, and Gold, a seasoned multi-instrumentalist and accomplished guitarist—effortlessly combining their distinct sensibilities for something hypnotic and tangibly inviting. What started as a love letter to their shared admiration for ‘60s and ‘70s Brazilian music evolved into a dynamic and sprawling body of work. These sunny and expansive tunes are as immersive as they are endlessly replayable.

Both Miller and Gold attended Oberlin College’s Conservatory of Music together and in the years after graduating, they orbited each other around Chicago’s music communities. “We were showing up for each other as friends and taking an interest in each other's projects, noticing a lot of resonances and similarities working within in our music,” says Gold, who’s collaborated with artists like Makaya McCraven and Jamila Woods and stretched the bounds of jazz and Americana on solo albums Imagined Sky and Midnight Choir. “We had talked so much about eventually working together that it was almost like an ongoing bit at a certain point,” says Miller. Though they had known each other for over a decade, they first had their chance on “Inside Minds,” the breezy lead single on 2023’s Resavoir. While those sessions were remote, two had palpable chemistry.

It wasn’t until Miller left the touring band of the Chicago group Whitney in 2023 that their plans to make music together in person came to fruition. “When I first started Resavoir, I was chasing the desire to produce records and now that I had time to focus exclusively on that, Matt was the first person I called to come to the studio,” says Miller. The two had bonded over an admiration for the Brazilian guitarist Luis Bonfa and songwriter Milton Nascimento, especially the latter’s work with Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter, so they decided to use nylon string guitar as a starting point for these early sessions. “Canopy,” which opens Horizon, was the earliest track. Kicking off with bright acoustic chords, the song slowly unfurls into a slinking groove, samples, and fluttering leads from soprano saxophonist Tim Bennett.

As these initial experiments proved successful, Gold and Miller felt they could broaden the scope of their vision. “We were initially conceiving of it as this acoustic guitar driven record but eventually we wanted to frame it orchestrally and see how many shades and colors we can bring in around that sound,” says Gold. “Dewy” thrives within this orchestral palette of woozy synths, strings from Macie Stewart, Claire Chenette’s oboe, flautist Wills McKenna, and French horns from Lloyd Billingham. “We discovered that our multi-instrumentalist mentalities—using piano and bass, samplers, drum grooves, guitar ideas all as starting points— nurtured the broad orchestration across this record,” says Miller.

“The LP took about a year with on-and-off sessions,” says Miller. “The songs benefit from letting them ferment for a couple months, coming back to it, and seeing what sort of new flavors have developed.” Co-produced by Miller and Gold (and mixed by Dave Vettraino), Horizon proudly reflects the artists’ vast artistic community and musical network in Chicago and beyond. Along with Gold, Eddie Burns (Clairo), Peter Mannheim (Tony Glausi), and Carter Lang (SZA, Lil Nas X) provide drums and percussion throughout. On the dreamlike single “Diversey Beach,” New York songwriter Mei Semones lends vocals and along with her band members Noah Leong and Claudius Agrippa, collaborated on a mesmerizingly conversational string arrangement. “We wrote "Diversey Beach" on the coldest day of the year watching a blizzard coming down out of the window, where the sounds of the cars driving by sounded like waves crashing on a beach,” says Miller. “I sent it to Mei Semones, who I’ve been a fan of for a long time. She's absolutely incredible and it’s amazing what she did with it.”

Horizon is a testament to the feeling of endless possibilities that come from collaboration. It’s a remarkable synthesis of two artists who share musical community and an artist lineage but have carved their own paths in unique ways. Nowhere is this more evident than “Hazel Canyon,” which boasts Gold’s silky pedal steel and a subtly enveloping arrangement that evokes Erasmo Carlos. “Musically, we're always trying to capture a fleeting moment of infinite expanse, feeling the vastness of things while knowing they'll always change,” says Gold. “This record keeps the light reflecting on the water just a little longer -- our collaborative process running through the backbone of these songs and rippling out in so many beautiful directions..””

items.body:
Oh man this is almost too much - just wall to wall genius in action courtesy of Floating Points & Eliot Bernard's Melodies International label -  spotlightling fire in the crown of Mad Professor’s pivotal London Lovers Rock and dub stable, Ariwa Sounds: from an immense monk-steppa ‘Non Violence Dub’ ft. Horace Andy, thru the Motown soul-infused Lovers of Davina Stone on 'Silly Wasn’t I’, to a Kofi gem recently found on Moin’s street-soul/digidub mix, the ruffneck charge of Mafia & Fluxy ‘6 Million Dub’, early Wild Bunch styles on Aisha’s ‘Can You Feel It’, and deadly ‘Liberated Woman’ voiced by Ranking Ann. All killer no filler!

“In 1979, Neil Fraser (artistically known as Mad Professor) founded Ariwa Sounds, the longest-serving and one of the most influential independently owned Reggae studios and record labels in the UK. From humble beginnings set up in the front room of Neil's home in South London recording on 4-track and homemade equipment, Ariwa would go on to record and release over 300 albums including works from some of the most impactful and storied artists of their time in the genres of Reggae, Dub, and Lovers Rock

Whilst our previous release in collaboration with Ariwa captured the label's early sound, a shared performance with Neil in Osaka and regular visits to his South London studio inspired us to assemble this 15-track compilation, showcasing the label's output across 45 years. Our release emphasizes some of the label's greatest vocalists: Johnny Clarke, Sandra Cross, Kofi, U Roy, Sister Nancy, Queen Omega, Aisha, Garnett Cross, Abel Miller, Horace Andy and more — presenting the Motown and Stax influences in the Lovers Rock, but also provides a glimpse into the dubbier and more experimental side of the label, showcasing Ariwa's commitment to quality but also their personality, philosophy and their humour. Love songs, break-up songs, socially engaged songs, dub experimentations — this compilation is not a "best of" Ariwa but a diverse and honest celebration of the label through the lens of Melodies International.”

items.body:
30 year return of Model 500’s overlooked but killer comet, straddling classic late ‘80s and emergent ‘90s strands of deep 313 electro-techno.

One of the more distant stars in the Metroplex galaxy, Juan Atkins’ 1993 single tends to the more introspective, wide-eyed side of Detroit club music. ‘I See The Light’ places his signature over-the-shoulder vocoder in an aerodynamic answer to his late ‘80s electro classics, riddled with ‘Clear’-styled arps and wickedly woozy choral pads ideal for tempering a set between more boisterous gear.

‘Pick Up the Flow’ is more clearly in step with the deep techno sound he was concocting at the time (often with Moritz Von Oswald), but still whirring with electro mechanics, balancing glyding pads and vocal soliloquy for the first half, and weaving in more Eastern-oriented melodic tang on the 2nd part.

items.body:
Kurt Wagner's seventeeth album as Lambchop - drawing on gospel and centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response singing.

"Lambchop's seventeenth album Punching the Clown finds Kurt Wagner returning to first principles. Sparked by a late-night radio encounter with an unidentified gospel recording, Wagner fell deep into the world of "lined out singing" a centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response tradition in which a lone clerk leads a choir through hymns, word by unadorned word. That spirit of raw, communal voice shapes every moment of Punching the Clown: Wagner spent years studying great songwriters and relearning his craft from the ground up, whittling dozens of songs down to twelve. Recorded in three days with guitarist Andrew Broder, Justin Vernon on banjo, and a six-part choir assembled by Blake Morgan and engineered by Lambchop veteran Mark Nevers, the album is graceful, wry, and quietly devastating. Out August 21, 2026 on City Slang.

Produced by Ryan Olson and recorded August 25–27, 2025, at April Base, Wisconsin. The record was completed over three days and features Kurt Wagner (vocals), Andrew Broder (guitar), Justin Vernon (banjo), and a six-part vocal ensemble, with additional choir recordings in London and Minneapolis."

items.body:
Jahtari light the fuse on a bag of digidub sound system detonators by Jamaican producer Prince Riser, aka Robbie Reiser, ranging from low pressure skank to flying dread steppas and original vocal cuts by Sammy Gold & Madi Simmons, all heavily lathered in FX...

“Dub album full of sound system explosives by expert riddim tinkerer Prince Riser – hard rocking, spaced out Kawai synth digi bangers, hitting that sweet spot between analog and digital Reggae while drawing vibes from the legacy of Dread & Fred, Exterminator and Jammy.

Aside from the thunderous Dub epic “Through The Storm” Prince Riser’s debut LP is also featuring the killer vocal cuts “Poverty Ina Russia” by Sammy Gold – a super heavy depth charge of Sly & Robbie proportions – the soulful Wackie’s flavoured anthem “Keep On Trodding” by Madi Simmons (who sadly passed away in 2024) and the plonky digi stepper “Travelling Gal” by Prince Riser himself, each accompanied by a murderous Dub version.

With extra cosmic dust added by disrupt at the Jahtari home studio, “Through The Storm” is crucial gear for any sound system vinyl crate.”

items.body: From Finland with love. A couple of glasses of kossu, a book of Arto Paasilinna, a record of the hardcore punk legends Kaaos, and then a movie (Calamari Union, yes) of Aki Kaurismaki, our true Homeric hero, have always been more than enough to attest to our fascination with that wonderful country. But there's more: a record label that, with the icastic name "We Jazz," helps illuminate our music like a sonic aurora borealis. The operational branches are “We Jazz Records”, established in 2016 to present "cutting-edge music on the jazz continuum in various formats, with vinyl being the primary format," and its younger sibling, “Other Power,” "a platform of all great music that doesn't logically fall under the scope of We Jazz." Both labels are curated and designed by Matti Nives. Should it be not enough satisfactory, then know that a quarterly magazine (actually a real glossy volume with color photographs) guarantees you the best editorial coverage of jazz/free/impro music available out there. For those not yet familiar with Helsinki’s alleys, we'd like to map the area with three, red marked, albums from the catalog: Mike Reed, "The Separatist Party"; Cosmic Ear, "Traces"; and Pat Thomas & XT, "Strata, Act." Completely different records with an enormous musical profile as a common factor, they represent an artistic asset value able to guarantee immortality to any label. We Jazz's new initiative includes the digital release of 5 tracks per month by bands not part of its roster, for the benefit of Bandcamp subscribers, and the kick-off is provided by this compilation which, with volumes 1-3, covers the period from January through March. We are dealing with such a cornucopia of music that it's worth a quick overview of all the musicians involved. UUSI AIKA (Sammaltuka). Strings, harp, wind instruments, drive the listener towards Finnish woodland mythology, Indian raga-inspired colors and Asian minimalism. HENRIETTE EILERTSEN TRIO (Fly Ikaros). Flautist's new band delivers a captivating composition with balanced interactions that at the same time manages to be intimate and almost limitlessly expansive. LAU NAU (Kosmospyorat). Synth drones mesh with the sound of a living garden, bees buzzing along beneath singing birds while simple chords carry dreams on oscillating waves. FELIX ALEXANDER LYBECK (Slapat Allting Hem). The magic of a Nordic forest, strange, weird folk notes intertwined with indie intimacy, creating music that feels both grounded and unearthly. JYVASKYLA WORKSHOP BAND 1970 (Nadaswaram). A previously unissued post-bop gem, this concert captures a set of groovy, adventurous and exotic compositions that firmly placed Finland on the global jazz map. LINNEA TALP (She came out of the white fog). The pipe organ is pushed in an unusual manner that allows the instrument's character to be revealed, gently, patiently, as though being teased out of hiding. ALAN BRAUFMAN (Angels). Alto sax and flute, among the actors of the 70s "loft" scene in New York, he returns after a long hiatus to lead an all star team (Patricia Brennan, Luke Stewart and Chad Taylor) between post-bop and oriental influences. FYSIIKKA & KEMIA (Luontokokemuksia). “Rural psych-jazz improvisations by Finnish bastard sons of Arbete & Fritid". Or, free music beyond the threshold where Swedish prog and Finnish weirdness collide. PIETU ARVOLA (Kummallinen ilmestys). Experimental tools like the daxophone and a dual looper called Coquantus are used to process textures combined with modular synths. MARK HARWOOD (The Course of a Year). Australian born, Berlin based, he runs a platform that works at the intersection of experimental music, performance, literature and visual art. GARD NILSSEN ACOUSTIC UNITY (Acoustic Unity). The sound of the sublime trio wrapped in the brutalist architecture and the magnetic audience of Barbican Centre, London 2018, delivers sheer, top notch, jazz aesthetic. HATKA (Peace Piece). Free, electro-acoustic textures and raw impro for an intense and playful outcome by a Transatlantic ensemble of three seasoned improvisers. KADI VIJA (Hands). A vocal instrumentalist who treats the human voice as a horn or a rhythm machine, here accompanied by piano, synth, vibraphone and percussions. PHARDAH (Village of Skulls). Featuring veterans of the Finnish experimental music and free jazz scene, along with a younger generation drummer, to unleash a vigorous bass riff, eventually accelerating into a wild collective gallop. If you're looking for a way (one of a zillion…) to epitomize in 1 hour what “Free” in music means, this compilation could be the perfect spot to pitch your tent. For our part, we already put in the collimator Vol. 2, sure thing. Check it out on Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Intakt Records, 2026 Personnel - Kaja Draksler: piano; Petter Elder: bass; Christian Lillinger: drums. The modern creative European trio Punkt Vrt. Plastik — comprising Slovenian pianist Kaja Draksler, Swedish bassist Petter Eldh, and German drummer Christian Lillinger — releases its fourth album. All three artists contribute compositions, adhering to unyielding rhythmic intricacy and classical melodicism to shape music that bristles with provocative interplay, freedom, and heightened expressiveness. Draksler's " Yogen " thrives on a half-step-shifting, mystery-inducing pulse. The pianist opts for motivic figures while the drummer moves from erratic fibrillation to deliberate syncopated fragmentation. This taut flow is regularly interrupted by pacifying jazztronica sections that contrast with the more Rage Against The Machine-inspired thrill of the opening. While Eldh's " Mariatorget 87 " also takes a distinctly jazz path, Lillinger's "For Sybille" finds Draksler veering toward a modern classical direction, rich with intervallic friction. The classical influence runs throughout the album but peaks with Eldh's arrangement of " När Världens Hopp Förtvinat Stod ”, a Lutheran chorale written in 1589 by German clergyman and composer Johannes Rhau. Draksler's 4/4 minor-mode piano movements find perfect backing from bass and drums. The classical vein continues on " Mere Punkt ”, co-composed by Draksler and Eldh, but shifts sharply for Lillinger's skittish “ Vrt ", which closes the album with a gallant composure. Eldh's "Trip" is one of the most gripping pieces, unfurling an oblique groove under a defiant time signature. Despite the complexity, the trio locks together in a fantastic, hooked-up rhythmic flow charged with creative harmonic progressions and tension. If " EKV " sounds progressive and warped, " For A / Kompress " is lyrical, cyclic, and powerful, opening with a dreamy aura that, handled with a firm grip, gradually intensifies. Surprising is hearing the trio lean into a hard-swinging juncture on " Granular Navigation ". Lillinger, unapologetic about his triplet-based ride cymbal patterns, wrote the piece; he also offers methodical snare buzz rolls that color a more abstract passage built from clustered chordal angularity. Punkt Vrt. Plastik engages in absorbing conversations of rhythm and breath, threading in occasional head-nodding grooves that arrive with atypical shapes and feels. The trio continues to seek new perspectives on composition, taking a freewheeling approach throughout. Kompress even offers a wider lens, feeling thoroughly contemporary without burying its influences from other eras. It stands as a fine addition to the group's catalog of state-of-the-art albums. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Yogen ► 02 - Trip ► 07 - For A / Kompress ► 09 - När Världens Hopp Förtvinat Stod

items.body:
Singapore’s electronic music calendar is getting a double dose of heavy hitters, with ARTBAT and Dom Dolla set to make their respective headline debuts in the city at Pasir Panjang Power Station.

Presented by Collective Minds, Ukrainian electronic duo ARTBAT will take over the industrial venue on 17 October, while GRAMMY-nominated Australian DJ and producer Dom Dolla will follow on 27 November.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Collective Minds (@collectivemindsasia)

Formed by Artur Kryvenko and Vitalii “Batish” Limarenko, ARTBAT have built a global following with their melodic techno sound, pairing driving rhythms with cinematic synths and emotionally charged melodies. Their Singapore debut follows appearances at some of electronic music’s biggest stages, including Tomorrowland, Coachella, Ultra Music Festival, EDC, Awakenings, and Time Warp.

The duo made their Ultra Music Festival Miami Mainstage debut earlier this year and returned to Tomorrowland Belgium in July. They are also scheduled to perform on Tomorrowland Thailand’s Mainstage in December.

ARTBAT’s catalogue includes their reimagining of Monolink’s 'Return to Oz', as well as recent releases 'Fight Machine', created with R3HAB, Stylo, Eli & Dani and featuring NAIIM, and 'Take You There' with SIX40TWO. Beyond their own releases, ARTBAT founded UPPERGROUND in 2021, which has since grown from a record label into a large-scale event concept and made its Asian debut in Malaysia this year.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Collective Minds (@collectivemindsasia)

A month later, Dom Dolla will bring his signature house sound to the same venue for his first headline performance in Singapore. The show arrives amid a major global run for the Australian artist, following his sold-out debut stadium performance at Sydney’s Allianz Stadium last December and two sold-out nights at Madison Square Garden. He is also set to perform at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium in September.

Dom Dolla has also announced headline dates across North America and holds residencies at Hï Ibiza and LIV Las Vegas.

This year, he released Addicted to Bass (Dom Dolla Relapse), an official remix of Puretone’s 'Addicted to Bass', collaborated with Tiga on 'Don’t Worry Baby', and delivered an official remix of KETTAMA’s 'Comes & Goes'. His catalogue has surpassed 1.5 billion streams, while his accolades include a GRAMMY nomination, four ARIA Awards for Best Dance/Electronic Release, and the inaugural ARIA Global Impact Award.

ARTBAT tickets start from S$128++ per person, with General Admission and VIP Stage Pass options available. VIP passes include behind-the-DJ-booth access, fast-track entry, and entry to an exclusive area with a dedicated bar. Dom Dolla tickets will be available via Megatix, with the artist presale opening on 2 September at 10 AM SGT and general sales beginning on 3 September at 10 AM SGT. Click here to for ticketing to both shows.

items.body:
Post Malone has postponed the entire Asia and Australasia leg of his BIG ASS Stadium World Tour, affecting shows across Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

The run was due to include stops in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, South Korea, and Japan, before continuing through Australia and New Zealand. Promoters and ticketing platforms across several markets confirmed the postponements on 27 August, with full refunds being issued for affected shows.

In Australia, Post Malone has also pulled out of his scheduled Strummingbird festival appearances as part of the change to his touring plans.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation Malaysia (@livenation.my)

For Singapore fans, this means Post Malone Presents The BIG ASS Stadium World Tour will no longer take place at the National Stadium on 25 September as scheduled.

Ticketmaster Singapore confirmed that fans who purchased tickets through the platform will receive a full refund via their original payment method. Refunds may take up to 60 business days to be processed, with no further action required from ticketholders.

The announcement follows days of uncertainty around the Singapore date after its Ticketmaster listing was marked as “Currently Unavailable”. The show remains listed on the National Stadium page with that status.

The Singapore concert would have marked Post Malone’s first full-scale solo headline show in the country. He previously performed here as part of the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix entertainment lineup in 2023.

The tour supports his sixth studio album, F-1 Trillion, which marked a deeper move into country music while continuing the hip-hop, pop, and rock crossover that has defined much of his career.

No reason has been officially given for the postponement, and new dates have yet to be announced. For now, the shows are being described as postponed rather than cancelled, despite refunds being issued across several markets.

items.body:
The mystery has been solved! Anyma has been revealed as the final headliner for MARQUEE Race Weekend 2026 with the electronic music heavyweight set to make his first-ever Singapore appearance at MARQUEE Singapore on 10 October.

His addition completes the Marina Bay Sands megaclub’s three-night Race Weekend programme, joining Diplo on 9 October and Martin Garrix on 11 October.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

For Anyma, the show marks a significant first. The multidisciplinary project of Tale Of Us’ Matteo Milleri has become one of electronic music’s most recognisable live acts, pairing melodic techno with large-scale digital worlds, humanoid figures and cinematic visual storytelling.

While his recent productions have played out across massive venues and festival stages, his Singapore debut will bring that spectacle into a much closer setting. MARQUEE Singapore’s giant 8K LED screen will place fans right in front of Anyma’s immersive visual universe, offering a more intimate take on the scale and sensory impact that have become central to his shows.

The booking also adds another major electronic music draw to Singapore Grand Prix’s Formula 1 weekend, with MARQUEE and Marina Bay Sands continuing to bring globally recognised dance acts into the city during one of its busiest entertainment periods.

items.body:
James Reid is soaking up the moment on his latest release.

The Filipino singer-songwriter and actor has released 'Sunny Side', a new collaboration with producer and artist Luke April via Sony Music Entertainment. The alternative pop track pairs filtered drums and guitars with an easygoing rap section, capturing the freedom of having nowhere to be and simply seeing where the day takes you.

Beyond its carefree sound, 'Sunny Side' sees Reid finding confidence in defining freedom on his own terms.

“Yes, it’s about freedom, but it’s also about feeling untouchable,” Reid shared. “Who I am is not defined by what people think; it’s who I choose to be despite what people think.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by James Reid (@james)

The track came together during a week-long creative session in a makeshift outdoor studio, where Reid, April, and their collaborators leaned into improvisation and experimentation. April cited Dominic Fike's Sunburn and Jean Dawson's 'Bruiseboy' among the musical inspirations behind the release.

'Sunny Side' offers another taste of Reid's forthcoming album, honey, i'm home, arriving 10 September.

items.body: The stars appear first. Their light seems to have traveled through the interior of a violin before reaching us, gathering the grain of wood and the pressure of a human hand along the way. Throughout Maksimal, Daniel Temkin thus treats music as celestial mapmaking, drawing places where the horizon turns out to be an instrument played from both sides. The title composition, written in 2022, carries the genetic traces of the Baroque concerto grosso into a world of fractured memory and unstable terrain. Francisco Fullana is the violin soloist, giving the music its incandescent center. Ryan McAdams conducts the Maksimal Ensemble with a keen understanding of the score’s shifting scale, allowing its smallest gestures to retain their mystery even as the orchestral field opens around them. “White Heat” begins with bells and glockenspiel drawing an aperture through which the violin’s restless language can spill across the page of the sky. Images arrive with a precision unavailable to the crude constellations of ordinary imagination, bearing the spirit of something immeasurable yet intimately knowable. Temkin’s orchestration blooms in radiant layers, creating enough space for the violin to run and fly without severing its connection to the ensemble. Fullana’s virtuosity serves as a vehicle for the music’s spirited intelligence, while winds and percussion orbit his line, occasionally catching its light. “Continuum” begins with the violin alone, carving space from time with resolute purpose while scarcely disturbing the air around it. As the orchestra unfolds along the periphery, molecular connections form between vanished cities and the people who once carried those urban spaces inside them. The piano exhales, while the brass catches and draws that breath underground. Though relatively brief, the movement produces the peculiar sensation of arrival. “Circle Games” then opens in buoyant motion before pivoting into contemplation, tracing a recurring exchange between outward momentum and inward gravity. The music brushes against the open-spaced pastoralism one might associate with Copland, yet its landscape keeps slipping beyond the trappings of such comparisons. Dreamed Landscapes, composed between 2017 and 2018 and rendered joyfully by pianist Ryan MacEvoy McCullough, brings this cartographic impulse into a more private cosmos. “Starfield” welcomes us into light as darkness’s fullest utterance, an illumination generated from within the black fabric itself. Dance-inflected steps puncture that fabric and reveal flashes of an alien expressivity, briefly exposing a grammar whose syntax exceeds the human nervous system. The suspicion of otherness soon becomes one that consciousness has always been plural. In “Glaciers crumbling, assembling,” the title’s entropy enters immediately through blocky textures and splintering masses. Fragments break loose from an immense harmonic body, while reformation becomes audible only in the ensuing silence, in which absence begins arranging the wreckage into a structure the ear can enter but never see. “Echoes of the Horizon” draws the cycle’s luminous points into its large-scale dissolutions. The insistent left hand establishes the fundament, while the right hand opens the firmament, hurling packets of emotional voltage across the distance between them. Under McCullough’s touch, the piano becomes a machine for folding vastness until mountains and oceans briefly occupy the same trembling surface. Ocean’s Call, composed in 2015 and revised in 2021, is a string quartet inspired by Big Sur and its environs. The Aizuri Quartet performs it with grace and exacting acuity, preserving the music’s sensuousness without softening its strange geological awareness. In “Hanging Cliffs, Rising Mist,” the cello draws a taut rope of purpose through the texture as the higher strings make room for a rising sun. Pizzicato details become lunar phases, while gradual coalescences deepen the field and pull the listener toward “The Bitter Salt of the Sea.” This central movement speaks in whispers, each phrase carrying the friction between water and air. The strummed cello sends tremors toward the crests of the waves, and the developing urgency becomes a form of surrender with a pulse still beating inside it. Temkin understands that yielding can possess enormous force and allows the music to lean into that paradox until submission and propulsion become indistinguishable. “Lullaby Waves” carries traces of Chinese folksong into harmonizations of light, setting them aboard a vessel woven from tenderness. As it travels farther across the water, the vessel gradually sheds the jurisdiction of the visible world. Across this recording, Temkin teaches the ear to draw maps, then quietly removes the territory beneath the pencil. Memory emerges as the architect of dimensions in which the vanished can continue to resonate. The sky finally collapses into the dark anatomy of listening itself, pierced by the patient apertures we once mistook for stars. The post Daniel Temkin: Maksimal appeared first on Sequenza21.

Consisting of one extended piece, the record captures a May 2025 live performance that the three artists did together at London's Cafe OTO. The set saw the trio reimagine a key vocal work of Palestine's, Karenina, which he originally recorded in Paris in March 1997. In this version, O'Sullivan controls three cassette machines playing the original recording, and also plays viola, synths and adds live vocals. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is something distinctive that makes Hiromi a jazz pianist whose albums transcend the genre; she grew up listening to 70s fusion and progressive bands, incorporating those harmonies into her music. Consequently, with her group Sonicbloom, those "spacey" explorations and ethereal sounds became more prominent, heightened by the presence of David Fiuczynski, an exquisite avant-garde guitarist whose style defies simple categorization, though it undoubtedly reflects the legacy of Allan Holdsworth. With this group, she created a concept album for her debut centered on the theme of time, as evidenced by the titles of the tracks."Time Difference" possesses both classical sensibility and the surgical, energetic precision of King Crimson. It engages the piano in a dialogue with the drums and guitar, then shifts to keyboard work accompanied by the electric bass."Time Out" features a funkier, more urban and cosmopolitan Groove, evoking a nighttime cocktail hour amidst marquee lights, the din of the crowd, and the sounds of traffic, while the guitar plays dissonant scales and the piano and bass cut through the air with tightly interlocking notes. The band becomes the soundtrack to a New York party, and the balance between experimentation and pure listening pleasure reaches its peak.A tranquil atmosphere with an Oriental feel, as if the spirit of Ryuichi Sakamoto had drifted in through the window, permeates Time Travel; naturally, the influence of Chick Corea's groups, such as Return to Forever and the Elektric Band, is also present. Hiromi is a fine exponent of "progressive jazz," though a different kind than that found in bands like Graham Parker's Strata or Red Kite. David Fiuczynski can play jazz, funk, or the more daring styles heard in Screaming Headless Torsos (another of his bands), while Hiromi continues to play and experiment with sounds alongside the band; at times they sound like a 1970s jam session, shifting to an 80s vibe, and finally landing on 90s fusi�n, a fitting progression, given that the album revolves around the concept of time."Deep Into the Night" reveals another, purely jazz-oriented dimension; it also offers a perfect opportunity to recommend her album with Stanley Clarke, where her piano prowess transcends mere virtuosity to convey ideas and emotions, capturing the spirit of classic jazz that she revives, offering the best of both worlds.A concept difficult to define, that chasm between what one feels and the divide between internal and external reality, is explored in "Real Clock vs. Body Clock = Jet Lag," a track where the meter is as complex as the message itself. Fiuczynski's guitar sounds as if it were melting in the midst of a surrealist act, yet at times she plays as if she were back in the 1920s. "Time and Space" is another gem (the entire album is, truth be told) and reminded me of another master well worth recommending: Misha Mengelberg and his album "Who's Bridge". In that trio setting with Daryl Jones and Joey Baron, they play with time and surprises much like Sonicbloom does here.Classical music takes time by surprise, and a fugue kicks off "Time Control" (or "Controlled by Time"), naturally bringing to mind Keith Emerson, who inhabited that same intersection of classical and jazz, before the band pulls us into the present; the Rhodes piano climbs powerfully alongside the group, reaching the very peaks of the genre and transcending them, with Fiuczynski playing his fretless guitar.Time Flies offers another moment to catch one's breath, a space where a sigh rises toward the sky, mingling with rooftops and treetops, for this album encompasses both day and night! Adventure transforms into fun and reflection; concept albums can be a delightful experience, culminating in an epic finale and the track "Time's Up" (which features a bonus track on the Japanese edition). Here, the band flows like a river, leaving genres behind on the Banks, held back by the stones, until only the purest, most transparent music remains.

items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — Well, They LOOK "Normal"!Rick Whitehurst, I mean. Who, along with Krystal Pavlovic, have composed and performed "Spider", under the 'current' name of BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL.I say 'current', since as you can plainly see, if you actually do look at the fine- and not so fine- print, that there is also the "EX BAKU LLAMA" moniker, as well as (if you query BAKULLAMA on ProgArchives, you will ALSO see BAKU), and yes, now "BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL".So maybe even the esteemed ProgArchives is confused.BAKULLAMA et alNear as I can piece it together- and I'm probably making way more of this than I need to, such is the burden of almost achieving OCD status- multitalented Rick has been at the heart of the BAKULLAMA enterprise since 2007, falling off the map (well, really, landing in Washington, resurrecting the music-making, with an impressive assortment of singles and albums in his/their discography.Of which, "Spider" is the latest release. And I found it meekly and humbly waiting to be reviewed, right here on the venerable ProgArchives.Patiently, seems to me.SpiderHere's (at least on Bandcamp) a nine track album.I say THIS, since you will notice (again, if you choose to peruse) the track list here on this site is only SEVEN tracks, almost all of them different versions than are to be found on Bandcamp, what can I say.And, to further complicate matters, even if on Bandcamp we can actually hear (I assume Krystal) singing in a husky and slightly world-weary manner, the only track that lists "lyrics", actually gives us the information: "none".The tracks that DO have lyrics, don't provide them.QuirkYes, the impression I need to impart is that although these two fine musicians APPEAR to be "normal" (and I'm willing to entertain as legitimate the observation you may choose to make, "What is normal"?), the music is rather a different tale to tell.For instance, in the ProgArchives forum inviting hapless reviewers to please take note of patiently waiting albums, someone (I just don't think it was Valdez, but who really knows), makes this statement: "It's a pop/electronic/prog hybrid of an album."Personally, I suspect Rick is behind this description, but I've been wrong before.I Couldn't ResistNo, this album is certainly eclectic, and certainly has electronica tones. There are some actual instruments, at least a Fender acoustic guitar and an Epiphone SG bass guitar are listed, and as far as I can tell, Krystal actually does use her actual vocal chords.These two pranksters eschew conventional forms and patterns, choosing instead to tempt and taunt the listener with sometimes spooky, odd, off-center, and just plain goofy fun while making music together.The liner notes say this seductively unusual commentary about "Spider": "A different and moody ode to Spiders, Birds, Mermaids... and Dreams."It's Just Cool, OKI like this. I think of "progressive", and it might at times mean "pushing boundaries", correct? It might mean breaking some rules and using off-beat humor and maybe sometimes, just not paying much attention to convention.Check. Check. Check.Anyhow, I'll not say more.C'mon. Take a chance! Who knows- a collection of nine, or six, or howEVER many tuneful explorations of zaniness MIGHT be just the ticket on such a day as this.My rating: 3.25 sarcastic stanzas out of a possible 5- good. And Slightly more than non-essential.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — These Arizona bros are definitely hooked on Krautrock ala Neu!, Can, Tangerine Dream and more of thekind. Soundscapes of Tangerine Dream, Cluster, early-Kraftwerk and the hypnotic "motorik" rock ofNeu! or Can. However, Trees Speak take 1970s German experimental rock & electronic music and puttheir own modern spin on them. Too bad they don't expand (read extend) more some of those greatideas (some of these tracks are way too short, IMHO), thus inducing a bit of a frustration in termsof depth - though this is never shallow, au contraire. One can only wonder if they'd dared plunginginto epic-length sonic explorations that Froese & Co. had done in their heydays.We've got a series of 16 short soundscapes (none over 4-mins) that are +/- fused into each other,and they transport you into the realms of synth and computer servers and other electronicsnightmares, and it's rather addictive, partly because there are real drums and a few more realinstruments played by guests (some will return on the next albums). The middle of the album , fromSadness of Wires until the title track is one amazing trip in copper and silicium. AFAIAC, my favetrack is Chamber Of Frequencies, where 'trons and and guitars create a special little plus.Though the following albums are of the same ilk, I must that none of them have resonated as muchwith my eardrums as their debut Ohms, partly because the surprise is gone. Impossible to pull outthe CD for only one sole listen: minimum two or three plays and it usually remains close to the deckfor possible more spins before heading (finally) back into the shelf. My 3.5 stars are of course notobjective, because Post-Human probably deserve as much as their previous releases, but I can't helpbeing subjective, not having that "Wow" factor.

items.body: Review by ProgExpert — It is amazing to hear H�llas go fully prog on *Panorama*. The record feels broader, more ambitious, and more mature than ever, while still retaining the melodic instinct and personality that make the band distinctive. I only wish a few especially beautiful musical ideas had been explored further, particularly the passage around 3:30 in the first suite and the wonderful final theme at the very end of the last song. Those moments are so strong that I wanted them to keep unfolding. It is brilliant to hear these artists growing in ambition and maturity. We simply cannot have enough of this music.

items.body: Review by ProgExpert — This is a remarkably delicate and sensitive record, played with exceptional taste throughout. Every arrangement feels carefully judged... nothing is overstated, and the musicianship is consistently impressive without ever becoming showy. There is a warmth and naturalness to the playing that gives the music an almost timeless quality! At several moments, it recalls the more pastoral and adventurous side of 1970s Caravan, with that same combination of melodic richness, subtle complexity, and effortless flow. What stands out most, though, is the restraint. Beautifully performed, elegant, and deeply musical. I cannot get enough, I wish they had composed 10 records! Not just 2! Come back Jouis!

items.body: Review by ValeriyK — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeOMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time continues the story started with OMNI, released by Antony Kalugin in 2025. And, without any doubt, OMNI II is one of the brightest progressive rock releases of 2026.A wonderful cast of musicians, clear and rich production and, most importantly, strong melodies make OMNI II a very enjoyable album from beginning to end. There is a lot of good music here, and I have already returned to this album many times.Like the previous OMNI, the music is divided into larger chapters. Here we have OMNI Part 4, Part 5 and the bonus Part 6, each approximately the length of one vinyl side.OMNI Part 4The album opens with The Glass of Time Part 1, and what a pleasure it is to hear Rob Reed here. For almost the first minute and forty seconds, it is basically Rob's world: keyboards, guitars and bass. Then Michel St-P�re and Antony Kalugin join in and the piece develops into a wonderful instrumental with a strong classic Genesis and Tony Banks flavour. It is a beautiful and very natural opening to the album.The second track, Frozen Rivers, is without doubt one of the highlights of the album. Here we meet the wizard Roine Stolt, one of the finest composers and guitarists in modern progressive rock, together with his brother Michael Stolt on bass. There is a very strong Scandinavian feeling running through this composition. Kalugin has mentioned that he wrote this song especially for Roine, and even the lyrics seem to reflect that connection.It is also a pleasure to hear John Hackett again on flute and Marek Arnold on soprano saxophone. Everything comes together beautifully, and the lyrics have a warm and soulful quality. For me, this is one of those tracks that immediately makes you want to press repeat.Then comes Shadowbound, and this is simply a hit. In another musical universe I could easily imagine this song appearing at Eurovision and doing very well there. It has an immediate melody and a memorable chorus, but underneath that accessible surface there is still plenty happening.The song deals with destiny, our choices and the struggle between different sides of ourselves. Mariya Panasenko is the real star here. Her performance is powerful, emotional and technically excellent, while Jannica Lund adds beautiful backing vocals and Roine Stolt contributes guitar. In the middle the song suddenly opens into a symphonic art-rock section. Somehow Karfagen manages to put Eurovision and progressive rock into the same four minutes ? and it works!Part 4 closes with The Shape of Love, featuring Marco Gl�hmann of Sylvan. Marco is surely one of the most distinctive vocalists in contemporary progressive rock. His voice is immediately recognisable, and the emotional range he brings to a song is remarkable.Just as The Last Card was one of my favourite moments on the first OMNI, The Shape of Love is one of the strongest songs here. It is also nice to hear Kalugin writing so openly about love again. I sincerely hope Marco will return for the next chapter of OMNI, because his voice brings so much emotion to this music.OMNI Part 5Part 5 begins with the nine-minute Carry On, and my only complaint is that I wish it were even longer!This is warm, vintage progressive rock, somewhere in the world of Alan Parsons and Electric Light Orchestra, but still unmistakably Karfagen. Yogi Lang of RPWL provides his characteristic vocals, and the composition develops through two rather different moods. The first section is energetic, positive, almost feel-good prog, while the second becomes more balladic and has, to my ears, something of the spirit of classic ELO.Kalle Wallner, also well known from RPWL and Blind Ego, appears on guitar, and it is great to see these two Bavarian musicians together on a Karfagen album. Michael Stolt once again provides his strong and dependable bass work.Beyond the Mirror brings back Per Malmberg, whom listeners of the first OMNI may remember from The Spark. Pascal Gutman adds Chapman Stick, and the result is another melodic and very positive song.And finally we hear Antony himself singing a verse! One thing I noticed on this album is that there is actually not very much lead vocal from Kalugin. Of course this is his artistic decision, but personally I enjoy his voice and hope to hear more of it on future albums.There is also a lovely moment in the middle of Beyond the Mirror where Jannica Lund's backing vocals meet acoustic guitar. Believe it or not, it reminds me of Fleetwood Mac ? that old, warm, soft pop-rock feeling ? and it fits surprisingly well.How Fragile We Are is a charming, enveloping and very gentle ballad. Mariya Panasenko sings beautifully, while Marek Arnold's soprano saxophone almost answers her voice like a second singer in a duet. Antony can also be heard on backing vocals in the chorus.There is something very Gilmour-like and Pink Floyd-like about the atmosphere here. Nothing is rushed. The song simply breathes, until we are left with the words: "Oh, how fragile we are?"The main album then closes with The Glass of Time Part 2, bringing us back to Rob Reed. Once again, for roughly the opening minute and forty seconds, Rob carries almost everything himself ? keyboards, guitar and bass. :)It works like a mirror of The Glass of Time Part 1, bringing the main album full circle. This is Karfagen instrumental music in its natural territory, with another gentle touch of Genesis and Tony Banks. A wonderful ending to the main 48-minute album.But fortunately, the CD does not stop there.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent CompassInstead of releasing another separate Working Tapes disc this time, Kalugin has included the complete OMNI Part 6, lasting just over nineteen minutes, as a bonus chapter on the CD. This material has also been announced as a separate digital release titled The Silent Compass, coming to streaming platforms this Friday. But CD listeners receive the whole additional chapter together with the main album. Thank you, Antony!It begins with Under the Northern Lights, a tiny piece lasting less than two minutes, but what a beautiful two minutes they are. This is almost classical music: piano, organ and orchestral colours, soprano saxophone, Roine Stolt's guitar and John Hackett's flute. There is something of Edvard Grieg in its atmosphere, perfectly matching the northern mood suggested by the title. A miniature symphonic pleasure.Then we arrive at The Silent Compass, one of the finest instrumentals on the whole release. Roine Stolt and Roberto D�az of Anima Mundi create a wonderful dialogue between their guitars. Max Velychko provides excellent acoustic guitar and John Hackett opens the piece beautifully on flute.There are shades of Anthony Phillips and The Flower Kings here, but ultimately this is Karfagen doing what Karfagen does best: melodic, pastoral and symphonic progressive rock with plenty of space for the musicians to tell their own stories.OM

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Really 4.75, but clicked 5...4 is too low.Quivira are new prog band consisting of: ?Jake Livgren (Emerald City Council, Kerry Livgren Band, Proto Kaw?he's Kerry's nephew) on lead vocals, ?Composer Lisa LaRue (RematriNation, Solo, 2KX, Federico Fantacone), on keyboards and programming, and ?John Baker (Forever Twelve, Mars Hollow, Little Girls) on guitars, bass and vocals. There are two guest performers: - Joe Deninzon (Kansas, Stratospheerius) / violin (5)- Evan Stanley (Stanley-Simmons?Paul Stanley's son) / guitar (9)According to the press release:This project blends historical themes, classic rock, and cinematic progressive rock into multi-movement works that emphasize narrative cohesion, harmonic exploration, and textural depth. The debut focuses on the story of pre-Kansas "Quivira", the Native American villages that Coronado believed held gold.This album comes courtesy of Nick Katona of Melodic Revolution Records (MRR). As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Track 1 - (Intro) The Coming of the Spaniards (3:52)A blend of vocal and string sounds provides a cinematic beginning, joined by drum accents. This feels like the beginning of an epic movie. Acoustic guitar gradually enters the soundscape along with the choral and orchestral themes. The acoustic guitar becomes more prominent as we proceed. A grand introduction!Track 2 - The Benefits of Breathing Quietly (5:55)The music quiets down to a single violin-like sound, then piano, bass and percussion enter. Jake Livgren enters on vocals with a very expressive melody. There are wonderful harmonies as the verse continues to build. The piano parts are absolutely beautiful as a synth solo enters soon after. The sound is warm and full; great production. Jake's vocals are exceptional! Not to play too heavily on the Kansas connection, but he is reminiscent of Steve Walsh in his prime. Lisa LaRue's synth solo is fantastic. The drum programming has some nice fills and syncs nicely, but I would always prefer a live drummer. Outstanding piano work as the song nears its conclusion. Jake closes it out with more top-notch vocals. Fantastic track!Track 3 - The Plains Truth (6:49)A quiet piano starts things off here. I believe the violin is synthesized, but it's convincing. This album is very dynamic! We get into a nice 6-8 groove here. John Baker has a nice guitar solo, making good use of delay effects. This is a wonderful instrumental track! Baker plays an acoustic solo at around 5:45 as well. Lisa LaRue shows her strengths here, not only as a terrific keyboardist, but an amazing composer and arranger. Another great piece of music! Track 4 - Quivira Bound (5:31)This begins with a prog-tastic intro with the synth in the spotlight, followed by acoustic guitar. Jake returns on vocals at around the 40 second point. I love the accents and harmonies as it approaches the chorus. This is glorious! The synth fill before the second verse is outstanding. Again, I hate to compare too much, but this really does remind me of classic Kansas. The "violin" solo could be Robbie Steinhardt. A strong guitar solo from Baker follows. I'm loving this track!Track 5 - Moving Forward (6:49)This commences with a brisk 6-8 and moves through several odd meters. This is the track on which current Kansas violinist Joe Deninzon appears, and his presence is felt early. This track will appeal to fans of prog with lots of meter changes. Joe's violin sounds like it's being fed through a distortion pedal, and even a wah-wah at times. Baker has a super-cool guitar feature after that. LaRue's piano continues to impress. Even the drum machine parts are solid and fit perfectly. This is another instrumental-only track, and it's amazing! Track 6 - The Turk - Follow the Wind (5:37)A syncopated piano part starts us off here. The vocals have adopted an accent, presumably that of "The Turk". A drum-groove and bass enter at around 1:25 to help propel the momentum. Nice change of pace into the chorus. The "violin" parts sound so realistic, I'm surprised it's not Joe Deninzon throughout the album. The solo that closes out the track is evidence of that. There are some sound effects at the tail end. This is another spectacular song!Track 7 - Nothing Is Everything (7:31)This one gets going with a high energy intro not unlike "No One Together". Again, I apologize, but this REALLY sounds like classic Kansas, while still being original?maybe it's just the setting of the music, but it really evokes that vibe. The intro consumes the first 3-minutes of the track, but I doubt anyone will mind! That was incredible! Things quiet down and become calm following the intro. There is a slow-build beginning at 3:45. I think this is another instrumental. Again, the dynamics on this album are incredible! LaRue's piano at 5:45 is nothing short of masterful. An acoustic guitar solo follows. Another stunningly awesome piece of music!Track 8 - Carved From the Sun (8:01) A mid-tempo introduction starts off this longest track. I like the bass line. The musicians have layered beautiful melodies and harmonies over the rhythm section. The tempo picks up at 1:40. This one rocks hard! Yet, that's not all it does. The arrangements throughout this album have been impressive; every bit is right where it should be. I think Jake is sitting this one out, too. Lisa and John have crafted some amazing instrumental prog here. Track 9 - Kicking Rocks (4:18)This is the track on which Evan Stanley plays. I have to say that when I learned that KISS' Paul Stanley's son was playing on this, I didn't see THAT coming! Piano and bass open the track, and the drums soon enter. Great bass line from John Baker. Evan Stanley's guitar playing is excellent. He and LaRue alternate between guitar and piano breaks. I like the blend of piano and synth. Stanley's main feature seems to be at around 3:00, and it's quite good. Track 10 - Prelude to Anywhere - Weekend Conquistadors (5:42)LaRue's fluid piano lines bring us into this track. After a cinematic opening, some short guitar riffs tease us. More masterful playing from LaRue follows. Hey, Jake's back at 2:40. He's accompanied by piano only at first, then the rest of the "band" kicks in for the chorus. And it's a great chorus at that! I love the lull then crescendo with about a minute left. Things quiet down, then there are spoken words:Male voice: "I will go to the end of the earth for that which I seek."Female voice: "True gain in life is not measured by the things we accumulate, but by the peace we possess."Awesome track!Track 11 - Still Breathing (5:58)Beautiful piano and violin take us into the final song. At around 40 seconds, big accents help amp up the energy. At 1:15, the music temporarily pauses. Shortly afterward, the beat kicks in for some wonderful melodies. I believe this is another instrumental track to close out this fabulous album. Tempo and mood changes abound! This one is quite cinematic as well. As the track fades out a horse neighs and trots off. A terrific ending!OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I keep having to say what an amazing year this has been for prog rock! I thought 2025 was great, which it was, but this year is phenomenal! Quivira have entered the running for prog album of the year here as well! What a debut! Certainly, a contender for best new prog band! My only nit-pick is that I would have preferred a live drummer. That said, the drum machine programming is very well-done. Lisa LaRue has established herself as a premiere composer, arranger and keyboardist. I am blown away. I was already familiar with Jake from his work with his uncle and even more so with Emerald City Council, but he really knocked me out with his performances on this album; spectacular. John Baker's bass parts and, especially his acoustic solos are quite tasty. I give this a nearly perfect 4.75 out of 5 stars (95%). Fans of symphonic classic prog will love the hell out of this album!

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Masterpiece from a band at the height of its creativityI have known A Night at the Opera since my teenage years, when it became one of my favorite albums. I first heard it through my father during family road trips, and those memories are certainly one of the reasons why this album remains so special to me. The fact that I did not approach it with any particular expectations and simply discovered it naturally makes my relationship with the record even more personal.For me, A Night at the Opera is one of Queen's best albums. It is remarkably consistent, with no weak tracks, and it perfectly represents many of the elements that made the band so distinctive during the 1970s. Hard rock, rock opera, pop, folk influences and theatrical arrangements are all present here, creating an extremely varied but cohesive album.I would not call A Night at the Opera a progressive rock album, but it undoubtedly contains several progressive elements. The clearest example is 'The Prophet's Song', probably the most progressive composition on the record. Its unusual structure, extended length, dramatic changes in atmosphere, complex vocal sections and ambitious arrangements give it a much more progressive character than the rest of the album. The famous vocal canon in the middle of the song, with multiple overlapping voices creating an almost hypnotic effect, is particularly impressive. The track also develops through different sections rather than following a simple verse-chorus format, making it one of the most adventurous compositions Queen ever recorded.The album's production and arrangements are also among its greatest strengths. Even without being an expert in production, it is impossible not to notice the enormous amount of detail in the record. The layered vocal harmonies, guitar overdubs, theatrical arrangements and constant stylistic changes create a rich and almost cinematic sound. This is an album that rewards repeated listening because there always seems to be some new detail to discover.Freddie Mercury delivers some absolutely beautiful vocal performances throughout the album. In my opinion, he had the greatest voice in rock music, and A Night at the Opera offers plenty of evidence for that opinion. Brian May's voice on ''39' is also a highlight, perfectly fitting the song's folk rock atmosphere, while Roger Taylor's more aggressive vocals make 'I'm in Love with My Car' a strong hard rock track.The album opens brilliantly with 'Death on Two Legs', an aggressive combination of hard rock and theatricality that immediately displays one of Queen's greatest identities during the 1970s. 'Lazing on a Sunday Afternoon' is one of the most unusual songs on the album and has a very distinctive character, while 'I'm in Love with My Car' brings a more direct hard rock approach and is also a perfect song for a road trip.'You're My Best Friend' is another extremely memorable track, while ''39' is one of my personal favorites because of its wonderful folk rock character and Brian May's vocals. 'Sweet Lady' brings another excellent dose of Queen's hard rock side, while 'Love of My Life' is probably one of the more pop-oriented songs on the album and became one of Queen's most iconic compositions.'Good Company' is another fascinating and unusual track, difficult to place stylistically but similar in spirit to 'Lazing on a Sunday Afternoon' in its old-fashioned and theatrical approach.And then there is 'Bohemian Rhapsody'.For me, this is not only the best song on the album but the greatest rock song of all time. It deserves every bit of its legendary reputation. The combination of ballad, opera and hard rock was an extraordinary innovation, and the composition remains as impressive today as it was when the album was released. It is a true rock anthem, but its fame should not overshadow the fact that the song is also an incredibly ambitious piece of musical creativity.The transition from 'The Prophet's Song' into 'Love of My Life' is another of my favorite moments on the album. Although the two songs are completely different, their placement creates a memorable contrast and contributes to the album's dramatic flow.No track is weak here. Every song has its own identity, and the diversity of styles never makes the album feel unfocused. If anything, that diversity is one of its greatest strengths.In my opinion, A Night at the Opera stands alongside Queen, Queen II, Sheer Heart Attack and A Day at the Races as one of the best albums Queen ever made. It may not be a progressive rock album in the strict sense, but its ambitious compositions and willingness to experiment with different musical styles explain why it can appeal strongly to progressive rock listeners.More importantly, this is an album I associate with family road trips and my adolescence, which makes it personally significant to me. However, even putting nostalgia aside, I still consider it an outstanding record that deserves its legendary status.Recommended to every fan of classic rock.

items.body: Review by Trinity S — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeI recently received the new OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time CD directly from Antony Kalugin and, after several listens, I would like to share a few impressions.First of all, this album sounds great. The production, mixing and mastering are excellent: clear, warm and dynamic, with enough space for all the keyboards, guitars, flute, saxophone and vocals. I especially enjoyed listening to it on headphones, where many small details become more noticeable.A special mention should go to Aleksandr Murenko on drums. With so many well-known guests on the album, his contribution could easily be overlooked, but his playing is powerful, musical and very tasteful throughout.The list of guests is impressive, but fortunately the album never feels like a collection of separate performances. Musicians such as Roine and Michael Stolt, Rob Reed, John Hackett, Marco Gl�hmann, Yogi Lang, Kalle Wallner, Michel St-P�re and Marek Arnold all become part of the same musical world.And this really does feel like a world. The beautiful artwork, booklet and posters look almost like a map from a Tolkien fantasy universe. Together with the different singers, instrumental passages and recurring musical themes, OMNI II sometimes feels like a progressive rock opera.Among my personal highlights are Frozen Rivers, with its wonderful Scandinavian atmosphere and Roine Stolt's guitar, the beautiful The Shape of Love with Marco Gl�hmann, and the nine-minute Carry On featuring Yogi Lang and Kalle Wallner.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent Compass may be presented as an additional part of the CD, but to my ears this is absolutely not bonus or leftover material. It is a strong and complete chapter in its own right. I especially enjoyed the instrumental The Silent Compass, with its beautiful guitar dialogue and John Hackett's flute, and We Live While We Remember, a wonderful and emotional ballad featuring Jean Pageau. These are actually among my favourite moments on the whole release.There was another nice surprise in my package: The Spektral World of Prog ? Volume 2 sampler CD. It was a pleasure to hear some familiar names alongside bands and tracks that were completely new to me. Thanks to Antony for making these companion releases ? they are a nice extra for those who still enjoy buying physical music.Beautiful presentation, excellent sound, strong compositions and first-class musicianship. OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time is another very strong Karfagen album and one I will certainly return to.Five stars. Rock on!
